From the abstract of 'next-gen-scraPy: Extracting NFL Tracking Data from Images to': Second, we analyze the resulting dataset, examining the spatial tendencies and performances of individual quarterbacks and defenses.
From the abstract of 'next-gen-scraPy: Extracting NFL Tracking Data from Images to': We usea generalized additive model for completion percentages by field location.

From the abstract of 'next-gen-scraPy: Extracting NFL Tracking Data from Images to': We introducea Naive Bayes approach for estimating the 2-D completion percentage surfaces of individual teams and quarterbacks, and we providea one-number summary, completion percentage above expectation (CPAE), for evaluating quarterbacks and team defenses.

From the abstract of 'next-gen-scraPy: Extracting NFL Tracking Data from Images to': We find that our pass location data closely matches the NFL’s tracking data, and that our CPAE metric closely matches the NFL’s proprietary CPAE metric.

claim: From the abstract of 'Optimal Exploitation of Clustering and': We consider the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem and the contextual bandit problem with historical observations and pre-clustered arms.

From the abstract of 'Optimal Exploitation of Clustering and': The historical observations can contain any number of instances for each arm, and the pre-clustering information isa fixed clustering of arms provided as part of the input.

From the abstract of 'Optimal Exploitation of Clustering and': We developa variety of algorithms which incorporate this offline information effectively during the online exploration phase and derive their regret bounds.

From the abstract of 'Optimal Exploitation of Clustering and': In particular, we develop the META algorithm which effectively hedges between two other algorithms: one which uses both historical observations and clustering, and another which uses only the historical observations.
From the abstract of 'Optimal Exploitation of Clustering and': The former outperforms the latter when the clustering quality is good, and vice-versa.

Abstract: We consider the stochastic multi-armed bandit problem and the contextual bandit problem with historical observations and pre-clustered arms. The historical observations can contain any number of instances for each arm, and the pre-clustering information isa fixed clustering of arms provided as part of the input. We developa variety of algorithms which incorporate this offline information effectively during the online exploration phase and derive their regret bounds. In particular, we develop the META algorithm which effectively hedges between two other algorithms: one which uses both historical observations and clustering, and another which uses only the historical observations. Abstract: In this paper, we presenta new model for ranking sports teams. Our model uses all scoring data from all games to producea functional rating by the method of least squares. The functional rating can be interpreted asa teams average point differential adjusted for strength of schedule. Using two team’s functional ratings we can predict the expected point differential at any time in the game. We looked at three variations of our model accounting for home-court advantage in different ways. We use the 2018-2019 NCAA Division1 men’s college basketball season to test the models and determined that home-court advantage is statistically important but does not differ between teams.

Paper overview — 'Online Gambling of'. Abstract: Online gambling sites offer many different gambling games. In this work we analyse the gambling logs of numerous solely probability-based gambling games and extract the wager and odds distributions. We find that the log-normal distribution describes the wager distribution at the aggregate level. Viewing the gamblers’ net incomes as random walks, we study the mean-squared displacement of net income and related quantities and find different diffusive behaviors for different games. We discuss possible origins for the observed anomalous diffusion.

Abstract: In professional tennis, it is often acknowledged that the server has an initial advantage. Indeed, the majority of points are won by the server, making the serve one of the most important elements in this sport. In this paper, we focus on the role of the serve advantage in winninga point asa function of the rally length. We proposea Bayesian isotonic logistic regression model for the probability of winninga point on serve. From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': We introducea theoretical framework of elicitability and identifiability of set-valued functionals, such as quantiles, prediction intervals, and systemic risk measures.A functional is elicitable if it is the unique minimiser of an expected scoring function, and identifiable if it is the unique zero of an expected identification function; both notions are essential for forecast ranking and validation, andMM- andZZ -estimation.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': Our framework distinguishes between exhaustive forecasts, being set-valued and aiming at correctly specifying the entire functional, and selective forecasts, content with solely specifyinga single point in the correct functional.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': We establisha mutual exclusivity result:A set-valued functional can be either selectively elicitable or exhaustively elicitable or not elicitable at all.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': Notably, since quantiles are well known to be selectively elicitable, they fail to be exhaustively elicitable.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': We further show that the class of prediction intervals and Vorob’ev quantiles turn out to be exhaustively elicitable and selectively identifiable.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': In particular, we providea mixture representation of elementary exhaustive scores, leading the way to Murphy diagrams.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': We give possibility and impossibility results for the shortest prediction interval and prediction intervals specified by an endpoint ora midpoint.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': We end witha comprehensive literature review on common practice in forecast evaluation of set-valued functionals.

From the abstract of 'Forecast Evaluation of Quantiles, Prediction Intervals, and other Set-Valued': Keywords: Consistency; Convex level sets; Elicitability; Identifiability;MM -estimation; Random sets; Vorob’ev quantiles MSC 2020 Subject Classification: 62C05; 62F07; 62H11; 91B061

claim: From the abstract of 'Multi-Armed Bandits with': We considera multi-armed bandit framework where the rewards obtained by pulling different arms are correlated.

From the abstract of 'Multi-Armed Bandits with': We developa unified approach to leverage these reward correlations and present fundamental generalizations of classic bandit algorithms to the correlated setting.

From the abstract of 'Multi-Armed Bandits with': Rigorous analysis of C-UCB (the correlated bandit versions of Upper-confidence-bound) reveals that the algorithm end up pulling certain sub-optimal arms, termed as non-competitive, onlyO⁡(1) \mathrm{O}(1) times, as opposed to theO⁡( log⁡T) \mathrm{O}(\log T) pulls required by classic bandit algorithms such as UCB, TS etc.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': We explore adversarial robustness in the setting in which it is acceptable fora classifier to abstain—that is, output no class—on adversarial examples.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': Adversarial examples are small perturbations of normal inputs toa classifier that cause the classifier to give incorrect output; they present security and safety challenges for machine learning systems.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': In many safety-critical applications, it is less costly fora classifier to abstain on adversarial examples than to give incorrect output for them.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': We first introducea novel objective function for adversarial robustness with an abstain option which characterizes an explicit tradeoff between robustness and accuracy.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': We then presenta simple baseline in which an adversarially-trained classifier abstains on all inputs withina certain distance of the decision boundary, which we theoretically and experimentally evaluate.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': Finally, we propose Combined Abstention Robustness Learning( CARL ),a method for jointly learninga classifier and the region of the input space on which it should abstain.
From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': We explore different variations of the PGD and DeepFool adversarial attacks on CARL in the abstain setting.

From the abstract of 'Playing it Safe: Adversarial Robustness with an': Evaluating against these attacks, we demonstrate that training with CARL results ina more accurate, robust, and efficient classifier than the baseline.

Abstract: Efficient and interpretable spatial analysis is crucial in many fields such as geology, sports, and climate science. Tensor latent factor models can describe higher-order correlations for spatial data. However, they are computationally expensive to train and are sensitive to initialization, leading to spatially incoherent, uninterpretable results. We developa novel Multiresolution Tensor Learning ( MRTL ) algorithm for efficiently learning interpretable spatial patterns. MRTL initializes the latent factors from an approximate full-rank tensor model for improved interpretability and progressively learns froma coarse resolution to the fine resolution to reduce computation. Abstract: In this contribution, we study the interaction dynamics in the game of football–soccer in the context of ball possession intervals. To do so, we analyzea novel database, comprising one season of the five major football leagues of Europe. Using this input, we developeda stochastic model based on three agents: two teammates and one defender. Despite its simplicity, the model is able to capture, in good approximation, the statistical behavior of possession times, passes lengths, and number of passes performed. In the last part, we show that the model’s dynamics can be mapped intoa Wiener process with drift and an absorbing barrier.I

Abstract: We propose an agent-based model of collective opinion formation to study the wisdom of crowds under social influence. The opinion of an agent isa continuous positive value, denoting its subjective answer toa factual question. The wisdom of crowds states that the average of all opinions is close to the truth, i.e. the correct answer. But if agents have the chance to adjust their opinion in response to the opinions of others, this effect can be destroyed. Our model investigates this scenario by evaluating two competing effects: (i) agents tend to keep their own opinion (individual convictionβ \beta ), (ii) they tend to adjust their opinion if they have information about the opinions of others

claim: From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': In this work we developa new algorithm for rating of teams (or players) in one-on-one games by exploiting the observed difference of the game-points (such as goals), also known asa margin of victory (MOV).

From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': Our objective is to obtain the Elo-style algorithm whose operation is simple to implement and to understand intuitively.

From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': This is done in three steps: first, we define the probabilistic model between the teams’ skills and the discretized MOV variable: this generalizes the model underpinning the Elo algorithm, where the MOV variable is discretized into three categories (win/loss/draw).

From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': Second, with the formal probabilistic model at hand, the optimization required by the maximum likelihood rule is implemented via stochastic gradient; this yields simple on-line equations for the rating updates which are identical in their general form to those characteristic of the Elo algorithm: the main difference lies in the way the scores and the expected scores are defined.

From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': Third, we proposea simple method to estimate the coefficients of the model, and thus define the operation of the algorithm; it is done ina closed form using the historical data so the algorithm is tailored to the sport of interest and the coefficients defining its operation are determined in entirely transparent manner.
From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': The alternative, optimization-based strategy to find the coefficients is also presented.

From the abstract of 'G-Elo: Generalization of the Elo algorithm by modeling the discretized Margin of': We show numerical examples based on the results of the association football of the English Premier League and the American football of the National Football League.

From the abstract of 'Sentiment Correlation in': In this paper, we apply NLP techniques to understand news sentiment of 87 companies among the most reported on Reuters fora period of seven years.

From the abstract of 'Sentiment Correlation in': We investigate the propagation of such sentiment in company networks and evaluate the associated market movements in terms of stock price and volatility.

From the abstract of 'Sentiment Correlation in': Our results suggest that, in certain sectors, strong media sentiment towards one company may indicatea significant change in media sentiment towards related companies measured as neighbours ina financial network constructed from news co-occurrence.

From the abstract of 'Sentiment Correlation in': Furthermore, there existsa weak but statistically significant association between strong media sentiment and abnormal market return as well as volatility.

From the abstract of 'Sentiment Correlation in': Such an association is more significant at the level of individual companies, but nevertheless remains visible at the level of sectors or groups of companies.

Result reported in 'Sentiment Correlation in': Similar to Figure2 where negative events are shown to be associated with greater movement in group sentiment, we also observe that negative events also correlate with larger market movements.

Michael J. Lopez (NFL/Skidmore) argues in the tracking-data special-issue introduction that most historical NFL analysis, mainstream and academic, relied on public play-level data and omitted variables such as play call, game situation, and opponent strength, making findings more anecdotal than actionable; with player tracking data, analysts can better isolate skill and strategy.

Michael J. Lopez asserts that, in the absence of using the precise yardage needed for a first down, past findings supporting an aggressive fourth-down strategy may have been overstated; fourth-down strategy is used as a microcosm for why tracking data is needed in football analytics.

Sobkowicz et al. (1910.03400) estimate the role of chance in success by comparing empirical 100-meter dash data (a discipline with stringent control of external randomness) against an agent-based model where success depends jointly on intrinsic talent and unpredictable luck; they find a small but non-zero contribution of random luck to the performance of the best sprinters, which may serve as a lower bound for the role of randomness in other, less stringently controlled competitive domains.

Zuccolotto et al. (1912.10417) model basketball shooting-performance variability with a Markov Switching dynamic assuming two alternating performance regimes (rather than measuring performance level only), then model each player's variability against lineup composition as an ARIMA process with covariates and describe teammate interactions with network analysis tools to extrapolate positive and negative interactions between teammates.

Gerlach & Sornette (2004.09368) simulate a price process as a geometric random walk combined with jumps whose sizes are proportional to the bubble size (so jumps efficiently bring excess bubble prices back to fundamental value - efficient crashes); investment strategies maximizing expected log wealth (Kelly criterion) in this crash-aware setting behave like Kelly on geometric Brownian motion, outperform other methods long-term, and beat classical Kelly, with the primary source of outperformance being knowledge about the presence of crashes.

Gerlach & Sornette (2004.09368) find that knowledge of only the crash size, not the time of occurrence, already provides a significant and robust edge for crash-aware Kelly strategies, and their error analysis shows the method is robust to parameter variations.

Paper overview — 'Quantile Regularization: Towards Implicit Calibration of Regression Models Saiteja Utpala sait@cse.iitk.ac.in Piyush Rai piyush@cse.iitk.ac.in arXiv:2002.12860v'. Abstract: Recent works have shown that most deep learning models are often poorly calibrated, i.e., they may produce overconfident predictions that are wrong. It is therefore desirable to have models that produce predictive uncertainty estimates that are reliable. Several approaches have been proposed recently to calibrate classification models. However, there is relatively little work on calibrating regression models. We present a method for calibrating regression models based ona novel quantile regularizer defined as the cumulative KL divergence between two CDFs. Paper overview — 'Static and Dynamic Models for Multivariate Distribution Forecasts: Proper Scoring Rule Tests of Factor-Quantile vs. Multivariate GARCH Models Carol Alexander, Y'. Abstract: A plethora of static and dynamic models exist to forecast Value-at-Risk and other quantilerelated metrics used in financial risk management. Industry practice tends to favour simpler, static models such as historical simulation or its variants whereas most academic research centres on dynamic models in the GARCH family. While numerous studies examine the accuracy of multivariate models for forecasting risk metrics, there is little research on accurately predicting the entire multivariate distribution. Yet this is an essential element of asset pricing or portfolio optimization problems having non-analytic solutions. We approach this highly complex problem usinga variety of proper multivariate

Utpala & Rai (2002.12860, 'Quantile Regularization: Towards Implicit Calibration of Regression Models') propose calibrating regression models with a novel quantile regularizer defined as the cumulative KL divergence between two CDFs; unlike post-hoc calibration approaches, the method trains end-to-end with no additional dataset required and can be combined with any regression training objective. Empirically it significantly improves calibration for regression models trained via Dropout VI and Deep Ensembles, while the authors show post-hoc methods like Isotonic Calibration sometimes compound miscalibration.

The 'Static and Dynamic Models for Multivariate Distribution Forecasting' paper (2004.14108) evaluates forecasts of full eight-dimensional multivariate distributions (exchange rates, interest rates, commodity futures) using proper multivariate scoring rules - Continuous Ranked Probability Score, Energy Score, and Variogram Score - comparing static models (empirical distribution functions and a new factor-quantile model) against dynamic asymmetric multivariate GARCH-class models.

In 'Beyond Pinball Loss' (Chung et al.), the pinball loss at quantile level tau in (0,1) is defined for target y and prediction y-hat; the paper proves there always exists a quantile model g with lower pinball loss than any given model f on a dataset D but worse average calibration, so pinball loss is detached from calibration. Empirically, while pinball loss decreases on the test set, test calibration worsens (sharpness improves), and at the best validation epoch the solution is sharper than the true noise level.

Average calibration for quantile predictions is defined as p^{obs}_{avg}(p) = E_{x ~ F_X}[F_{Y|x}(Q-hat_p(x))] for all p in (0,1), i.e. the probability of observing the target below the quantile prediction, averaged over the input distribution, equals p. Its finite-sample estimate is p-hat^{obs}_{avg}(D,p) = (1/N) sum_{i=1}^N I{y_i <= Q-hat_p(x_i)}, and expected calibration error is ECE(D, Q-hat) = (1/m) sum_{j=1}^m |p-hat^{obs}_{avg}(D,p_j) - p_j| with p_j ~ Unif(0,1).

In Bingham's survey 'Prediction Theory for Stationary Functional Time Series', a stationary process x = {x_n : n in Z} in a Hilbert space admits the Cramer representation as a stochastic integral of an orthogonal-increments process: x_n = integral e^{in theta} dY(theta). The Wold decomposition splits x = x_d + x_p into deterministic and purely non-deterministic components that are Gramian orthogonal ([x_d(m), x_p(n)] = 0).

The Kolmogorov-Szego formula relates the Verblunsky coefficients alpha_k (in the unit disc) of a stationary sequence to its spectral density f(theta): product_{k=0}^{infty} det(1 - alpha_k alpha_k^dagger) = exp integral tr log f(theta) d theta / 2 pi. In the scalar case this gives the one-step prediction error variance sigma^2 = exp{ integral log f(theta) d theta / 2 pi } > 0.

A self-supervised pipeline detects and tracks low-resolution soccer players without any ground-truth data, by knowledge transfer from a pretrained general human detector (teacher) to a soccer player detector (student), keeping teacher annotations with confidence above sigma = 0.8. Both the detector and tracker achieve top-tier results versus state of the art, especially for small players.

The soccer tracking model is trained with a triplet loss over tracklets: L_triplet(theta) = sum_{k=1}^K sum_{t=1}^T [ m + max_{u} ||f_theta(b_t^k) - f_theta(b_u^k)||_2 - min_{i != k, u} ||f_theta(b_t^k) - f_theta(b_u^i)||_2 ]_+, with margin m = 2, and the final training loss is L = L_detection + L_triplet. For track association the cost between detections combines visual and spatial distances: C(b_t^i, b_{t_j}^k) = alpha D_visual + (1 - alpha) D_spatial with 0 <= alpha <= 1 (optimal alpha = 0.03 at inference).

Combining statistical match data with NLP features from Guardian match previews, a Random Forest ensemble (Model 4, combining text-model probabilities with bookmaker and Dixon-Coles probabilities) reaches 63.2% accuracy on English Premier League match outcomes (home win/draw/away win), a 6.9% boost over traditional statistical methods, 10.8% above bookmaker accuracy and 4.1% above Dixon & Coles. Without the text features, F1 is 10% lower and accuracy 7% lower. Text-only Model 1 reaches 53.5%, below Dixon & Coles.

The paper cites bookmaker prediction accuracies of about 67% for American football, 74% for basketball, 64% for cricket, 61% for baseball, and just 54% for football (soccer). Its model formalizes each game with outcome set O = {homewin, draw, awaywin}, feature set X = [mu . V(alpha), V(beta)] for home team alpha and away team beta, and target y predicted by Random Forest phi with phi(X) = y.

D'Agostini's didactic paper distinguishes the predictive problem (forecasting counts and their ratios under stated assumptions) from the inferential problem (learning the Poisson rate parameters from observed counts), visualized with a Bayesian network. The Poisson pmf is f(x | lambda) = lambda^x / x! . e^{-lambda} for x = 0,1,..., with lambda = r . T where r is the rate and T the observation time. For X_1 ~ P_{lambda_1}, X_2 ~ P_{lambda_2}, the difference D = X_1 - X_2 is expected to be (lambda_1 - lambda_2) +- sqrt(lambda_1 + lambda_2).

For small lambda_2, the ratio of Poisson counts X_1/X_2 has high probability of being undefined or infinite (exactly the probability of X_2 = 0), so the distribution of the ratio of counts is ill-behaved where the ratio of rates is the quantity of interest. Monte Carlo (10^6 samples, rpois in R) confirms the exact enumeration results, and approximate inference is shown via MCMC with JAGS/rjags.

In 'Limits of PageRank-based ranking methods in sports data' (Zhou & Wang, calibrated on 18 major leagues), PageRank outperforms the benchmark ranking by number of wins only when a small fraction of all games have been played; intrinsic outcome randomness and home-team advantage further shrink the range of PageRank's superiority. The authors propose a bi-directional PageRank variant that outperforms standard PageRank in all evaluated settings but shares its sensitivity to increased randomness.

The paper models the home team's win probability as a logistic function of intrinsic fitness difference plus home advantage: P(i,j) = 1/[1 + e^{-(f_i - f_j + H)/delta}], where f_i, f_j are team fitness values, H is home advantage, and delta is a weighting parameter; as delta -> infinity, P(i,j) -> 1/2 and outcomes become fully random. The sports PageRank prestige score is P_i = (1-alpha) sum_j P_j w_{ji}/s_j^{out} + alpha/N + (1-alpha)/N sum_j P_j delta(s_j^{out}), with alpha = 0.15, w_{ji} the number of wins of i over j, and s_j^{out} the number of losses of j.

For online golf ball detection/tracking, five CNN detectors (YOLOv3, YOLOv3-tiny, YOLOv4, Faster R-CNN, SSD, RefineDet) were evaluated with detection run on small image patches plus a discrete Kalman filter for location prediction. YOLOv4 achieved the best mAP precision, Faster R-CNN was comparable, and YOLOv3-tiny had 4-12x shorter inference time than the others; two-stage detectors (Faster R-CNN) dominate mAP while SSD performs poorly on small objects.

A spatial-temporal multi-agent trajectory prediction model uses a fully-connected graph with attention for permutation-equivariant agent dependencies plus a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) for parallelism and stable gradients instead of RNNs. On basketball and soccer datasets, attention-based variants (Graph + Attention + LSTM/TCN) largely outperform HMM + LSTM and Graph + VRNN baselines, and defense-team trajectory prediction improves about 8% over offense-team prediction.

In the graph-attention trajectory model, node embeddings are attention-weighted aggregations h'_i = sigma[sum_{j in K} a_{ji}^{(l)} . z_j^{(l)}], the graph embedding at time t is g^t = sum_{i in K} h'_i, and the temporal module applies dilated convolution C(s) = sum_i k(i) . g_{s - d.i} with dilation factor d and kernel size f.

In 'Beyond Strictly Proper Scoring Rules', strictly proper scoring rules need not rank imperfect forecast systems in the same order. The CRPS is shown to prefer outcomes close to the median of the forecast distribution regardless of the probability mass at the median, producing 'unfortunate' evaluations (implausible: p_A(Y)/p_B(Y) = infinity yet CRPS prefers p_B). The logarithmic score is the only local strictly proper scoring rule, has direct interpretation in probabilities/bits of information, and is invariant under smooth transformations of the forecast variable, while nonlocal rules can flip preferences under transformation; the log score should always be included in probabilistic forecast evaluation.

A scoring rule S(p(x), Y) is proper if integral q(z) S(p(x),z) dz >= integral q(z) S(q(x),z) dz for all forecast PDFs p, q (strictly proper if equality implies p = q). The Energy Score family is S_{ES}(p(x),Y) = E_p ||x - Y||^beta - (1/2) E_p ||x - x'||^beta with beta in (0,2), x, x' independent copies from p; beta = 1 gives CRPS. The Proper Linear (Quadratic) Score is S_{PLS}(p(x),Y) = -2 p(Y) + integral p^2(z) dz, and the Spherical Score at beta = 2 is S_{SPS}(p(x),Y) = -p(Y)/(integral p^2(z) dz)^{1/2}.

Elo-MMR is a novel Bayesian rating system for contests with many participants (ranked rounds like programming competitions, obstacle races, video games). It provably aligns incentives (a player maximizing rating never wants to underperform), comes with theoretical bounds on robustness and runtime, and experimentally rivals or surpasses existing systems in prediction accuracy while computing up to an order of magnitude faster.

Elo-MMR's Bayesian model factorizes the joint distribution as Pr(S_:,:,P_:,:,E_:) = prod_i Pr(S_i,0) prod_{i,t} Pr(S_i,t | S_i,t-1) prod_{i,t} Pr(P_i,t | S_i,t) prod_t Pr(E_t | P_:,t), where S_i,t is skill, P_i,t is round performance, and E_t is the round ranking. The rating is the MAP estimate mu_i,t := argmax_s pi_i,t(s) Pr(P_i,t | S_i,t = s) with skill prior pi_i,t(s) := Pr(S_i,t = s | P_i,<t); the performance posterior concentrates at the true P_i,t as the number of participants -> infinity via Doob's consistency theorem.

A parametric model predicts the probability of a football team scoring given it has taken a shot at goal, outperforming a model that assumes equal shot-success probability across teams; combined with GAP ratings that predict each team's number of shots, it increases forecast skill for both match outcome and whether total goals exceed 2.5. Forecast skill was also assessed alongside two betting strategies with mixed evidence for improved performance.

The shot-success paper defines climatological shot-success probability p_c = sum_{m=1}^M G_m / sum_m S_m (total goals over total shots), and a blended forecast p-tilde = alpha p + (1 - alpha) p_c mixing the model forecast p with climatology. Evaluation uses the Brier score Brier = sum_{i=1}^r (p_i - o_i)^2 and the Ranked Probability Score RPS = sum_{i=1}^{r-1} sum_{j=1}^i (p_j - o_j)^2 over r ordered outcomes.

In 'Rankings for Bipartite Tournaments via Chain Editing' (AAMAS), a bipartite tournament is a triple (A,B,K) with K_ab in {0,1}; chain graphs (nested defeated-adversary neighborhoods N(u_1) subseteq ... subseteq N(u_k)) induce natural rankings. Chain editing finds the closest chain tournament M(K) = argmin_{K' in C_{m,n}} d(K,K') under Hamming distance d(K,K') = |{(a,b): K_ab != K'_ab}|; these rankings arise as maximum likelihood estimators in a noisy probabilistic model, but chain editing is NP-hard and violates an anonymity axiom, both addressed by a relaxed greedy approximation.

A hierarchical Bayesian model describes shot-put athlete performance trajectories as noisy measurements of an underlying function: y_ij = g_i(t_ij) + epsilon_ij with epsilon_ij iid N(0, psi^2), decomposed as g_i(t_ij) = f_i(t_ij) + mu_{is} + x_i(t_ij) beta, where f_i is a smooth functional component via B-spline basis f_i(t) = sum_{m=1}^p theta_{im} b_m(t) with sparse latent-factor structure theta_{im} = sum_{l=1}^k lambda_{ml} eta_{il} + xi_{im}, and mu_{is} is an athlete-specific seasonal step function. Applied to elite professional shot-put data, it captures intra- and inter-seasonal variability and predicts future seasons.

The shot-put model places a GARCH-type conditional variance on the seasonal intercepts: mu_{is} | m, h_{is} = m + zeta_{is} iid N(m, h_{is}) with h_{is} = alpha_0 + alpha_1 zeta_{is-1}^2 + varpi h_{is-1} (alpha_0 > 0, alpha_1, varpi >= 0), where zeta_{is} = mu_{is} - m. Wide-sense stationarity with Var(zeta_t) = alpha_0 (1 - alpha_1 - varpi)^{-1} and Cov(zeta_t, zeta_s) = 0 for t != s requires alpha_1 + varpi < 1.

Under weak-signal asymptotics for sequentially randomized experiments (K-armed bandits), mean reward gaps scale as 1/sqrt(n) and the sample paths of experiments with arm-selection probabilities varying continuously with state converge weakly to a diffusion limit (solution of an SDE). All sequential experiments whose randomization probabilities depend Lipschitz-continuously on observed data suffer sub-optimal regret when reward gaps are relatively large; Thompson sampling with an asymptotically uninformative prior variance achieves near-optimal instance-specific regret scaling even with large gaps, at the cost of highly unstable posterior beliefs. UCB is excluded because it violates the continuity assumption.

Bandit regret is defined as R^n = n sup_{1<=k<=K} {mu_k} - E[sum_{i=1}^n mu_{A_i}] with mu_k = E_{P_k}[Y], and any sequential algorithm has expected regret lower-bounded of order sqrt(Kn). State variables are pull counts Q_{k,i} = sum_{j=1}^i 1{A_j = k} and cumulative rewards S_{k,i} = sum_{j=1}^i 1{A_j = k} Y_j; a tempered greedy rule samples arms with pi_{i,k} = exp[alpha S_{k,i}/(Q_{k,i}+c)] / sum_l exp[alpha S_{l,i}/(Q_{l,i}+c)], and Luce's rule uses pi_{i,k} = (S_{k,i} vee alpha)/sum_l (S_{l,i} vee alpha).

Automatic Model Selector (AMS) performs scalable online selection of real-time-bidding bidding strategies using multi-armed bandits: multiple models run and are evaluated near-simultaneously against live traffic, the most traffic goes to the best-performing models and traffic to poor models is decreased, minimizing inferior models' impact on campaign performance; in live-traffic tests on multiple ad campaigns AMS proved highly effective at improving campaign performance.

A deep-learning weather prediction (DLWP) ensemble system uses CNNs on a cubed-sphere grid to recursively predict atmospheric variables at 6-hour resolution; 320-member six-week ensembles at 1.4-degree resolution are produced in ~3 minutes on a single GPU, with ensemble spread from randomizing CNN training (32 DLWP models). The ensemble-mean RMSE retains skill vs climatology beyond two weeks, anomaly correlation stays above 0.6 through six days, and by CRPS/RPSS the DLWP ensemble is only modestly inferior to the ECMWF S2S ensemble over land at 4-6 week leads; it also spontaneously generates tropical cyclones in free-running simulation.

The DLWP paper uses the Continuous Ranked Probability Score CRPS(P, x_a) = integral_{-infty}^{infty} [P(x) - P_a(x)]^2 dx where P is the forecast CDF and P_a(x) = H(x - x_a) is the observation CDF with Heaviside H, plus the Ranked Probability Skill Score RPSS = 1 - <RPS>/<RPS_C> where RPS = sum_{k=1}^K (Y_k - O_k)^2 over cumulative category probabilities and RPS_C is the climatology counterpart.

Minimizing an expected pinball loss over a continuous distribution of quantiles is a good regularizer for quantile regression even when only predicting a specific quantile; non-crossing quantiles are achieved with deep lattice networks treating the quantile as a monotonic input feature, monotonicity on other features is an apt regularizer, lattice models enable regularizing the predicted distribution to a location-scale family, and rate constraints improve calibration on subsets of interest and fairness metrics (demonstrated on simulations, benchmarks, and real problems including air quality, traffic, wine, puzzles).

The quantile-regression paper fits f(x, tau; theta) by the constrained optimization min_theta E_T[sum_{i=1}^N L_T(y_i, f(x_i, T; theta))] subject to f(x, tau^+; theta) >= f(x, tau^-; theta) for all x and tau^+ >= tau^-, where the pinball loss is L_tau(y, y-hat) = max(tau(y - y-hat), (tau - 1)(y - y-hat)). The location-scale regularizer imposes F^{-1}_{Y|X=z}(tau) = a + b F^{-1}_{Y|X=x}(tau) for the conditional inverse CDFs.

The paper introduces quasi-arithmetic (QA) pooling of expert probability distributions: given a proper scoring rule s with Savage expected-reward function G (strictly convex) and gradient g, the aggregate p* satisfies g(p*) = sum_{i=1}^m w_i g(p_i). QA pooling w.r.t. the quadratic scoring rule reduces to linear pooling p* = sum_i w_i p_i, while QA pooling w.r.t. the logarithmic scoring rule reduces to logarithmic (geometric) pooling p*(j) = c prod_i (p_i(j))^{w_i}; online gradient descent can learn the expert weights with low regret.

Fujii's survey on data-driven team-sports behavior analysis identifies two main approaches: (1) extracting interpretable features/rules from data (visualizing learned representations, extracting mathematical structure), and (2) generating and controlling behaviors in visually understandable ways to test hypotheses by simulating future and counterfactual behaviors (e.g., RL-based evaluation of player/team actions and states). Trajectories are formalized as P = (p_1,...,p_m) with p_i in R^d, multi-agent trajectories P_K = (p_{K,1},...,p_{K,m}) with p_{K,i} in R^{K x d}, and relation sequences R_K = (R_1,...,R_m) with R_i in R^{K x K}.

Prediction intervals for regression are learned via the empirical constrained optimization opt-hat(t): min_{L,U in H, L<=U} E_{pi-hat_X}[U(X) - L(X)] subject to P_{pi-hat}(Y in [L(X), U(X)]) >= 1 - alpha + t, with adjustment t in [0, alpha] boosting generalized coverage (with t = 0, true coverage can fall below 1 - alpha with significant probability despite empirical coverage above it). Learning theory characterizes the optimality-feasibility tradeoff via Lipschitz continuity and VC-subgraph classes (exemplified by regression trees and neural networks), with deviation bound phi_1(n, epsilon, H) <= 2 exp(-n epsilon^2 / (C ||H||_{psi_2}^2 vc(H_+))).

'Flexible Model Aggregation for Quantile Regression' (Fakoor, Kim, Mueller, Smola, Tibshirani, JMLR) aggregates any number of conditional quantile models via weighted ensembles where weights vary over models, quantile levels, and feature values: g-hat_w(x) = sum_{j=1}^p w_j(x) . g-hat_j(x). It provides tools to keep quantiles monotonically ordered plus conformal calibration without modifying base models, proves post-sorting or post-isotonic-regression can only improve the weighted interval score, and runs an extensive empirical comparison across 34 datasets from two benchmark repositories.

The paper establishes the exact identity between CRPS and pinball loss: integral_{-infty}^{infty} (F(y) - 1{Y <= y})^2 dy = 2 integral_0^1 psi_tau(Y - F^{-1}(tau)) d tau, where the pinball loss is psi_tau(Z - q) = tau|Z - q| if Z - q >= 0 and (1 - tau)|Z - q| otherwise, minimized in expectation at the population quantile q*_tau = F_Z^{-1}(tau).

Predd et al. (2009) showed that for a finite sample space and any strictly proper additive continuous scoring rule, any forecast violating the probability axioms is strictly dominated by some probabilistically consistent forecast; this result was extended to non-additive continuous scoring rules, and this paper gives a condition weaker than continuity that still suffices for the dominance result and proves the condition is optimal.

The astroinformatics paper argues probabilistic redshift PDFs must be evaluated with proper tools: log-likelihood, CRPS, and the probability integral transform (PIT) for calibration and sharpness; using proper scoring rules to train deep neural networks led from well-calibrated redshift estimates to improved probabilistic weather forecasting. In a case study on temperature forecasts at more than 500 German weather stations, NN models consistently outperformed statistical and ML benchmarks. It warns of common conceptual mistakes in the literature, e.g. F-score improving when uncertainty is artificially shrunk while calibration shows severe underdispersion.

'Markov Cricket' (Vohra & Gordon) models one-day international cricket as a Markov process: Monte-Carlo learning fits a nonlinear value-function approximation with a score-based reward, and as a proxy for remaining scoring resources it outperforms the Duckworth-Lewis-Stern method by 3-10x (error range -2.11% to -0.11% vs DLS 2.77%-5.41%; best test -0.96% to 1.82% vs DLS 2.06%-4.54%; first innings -1.11% vs 4.27%). Inverse RL (guided-cost-learning variant) infers a linear reward model from winning-team play sequences whose optimal policy matches cricket intuition, and an MDP simulator yields the posterior distribution of final scores from any state.

Siamese neural networks combined with LightGBM/XGBoost for sports match-importance prediction and team ranking: triplet-loss models beat contrastive-loss models. LightGBM (triplet loss) is the most effective NBA ranker with state-of-the-art mAP 0.867 and NDCG 0.98; the SNN (triplet loss) most effectively predicted Super 15 Rugby with SOTA mAP 0.921, NDCG 0.983, and Spearman r_s 0.793. No single model is best across both sports.

The contrastive loss used in the sports similarity-learning paper is J(theta) = (1-Y)(1/2)(D_{a,b})^2 + (Y)(1/2)(max(0, m - D_{a,b}))^2 with Y = 0 for a win and 1 for a loss, margin m, and Euclidean embedding distance D_{a,b}(x_1,x_2) = sqrt(sum_k (b(x_2)_k - a(x_1)_k)^2). Gradient-boosting pseudo-residuals are r_{im} = -dL(y_i, F_{m-1}(x_i))/dF_{m-1}(x_i) and the ensemble updates as F_m(x) = F_{m-1}(x) + lambda_m gamma_m h_m(x).

A probabilistic weather-forecasting approach trains neural networks to predict full probability density functions at each point in space and time (continuous targets binned into 100 categorical bins), on WeatherBench/ERA5 data for geopotential and temperature 3 and 5 days ahead. Each network trains on a small subset of input variables and outputs are combined through a stacked neural network (first such application to weather data); the approach beats some numerical weather prediction models and matches more complex NN alternatives while providing uncertainty and skill metrics.

The weather-PDF paper evaluates with latitude-weighted RMSE = sqrt((1/N_timepoints) sum_i (1/(N_lat N_lon)) sum_{j,k} L(j)(f_{i,j,k} - t_{i,j,k})^2) where L(j) = cos(lat(j))/((1/N_lat) sum_j cos(lat(j))) is the latitude weighting factor, recovers expectations from predicted PDFs as E[X] = sum_{i=1}^{100} x_i P(X = x_i) with bin lower bounds x_i, and scores probabilistic forecasts with CRPS(F,y) = integral_{-infty}^{infty} (F(z) - 1(y <= z))^2 dz.

'Leaving Goals on the Pitch' (Van Roy, Robberechts, Yang, De Raedt, Davis, KU Leuven) proposes a generic ML/AI framework to evaluate soccer decision-making (e.g., shoot vs. move) via counterfactual policy alterations; decreasing the shooting probability by x percent in a state is realized as pi'(shoot|s) = (1 - x) . pi(shoot|s) with move probabilities renormalized. Results show per-team zones where moving beats shooting and vice versa, with an average relative error of 11.38% over all teams.

A refined ELO system for Skat (and trick-taking games generally) compensates for opponent strength and the luck of the deal, aligning with established tournament scoring via the Seeger-Fabian evaluation S = S_0 + S_1 + S_2 and rating R = R_0 + R_1 + R_2. To reduce the chance factor, a hand-strength function normalizes for the initial deal; player ratings initialize as R_i^{(n)} = sum_{t=0}^n S^{(t)}/n, and experiments on human game series derived proper ELO rankings across K-factor parameterizations.

Controlled Abstention Networks (CANs) for regression (Barnes & Barnes) introduce an 'abstention loss' applied during training to identify forecasts of opportunity and abstain ('I don't know') on low-confidence samples: L(x_i) = -q_i log p_i - alpha log q_i, where p_i = N(y_i; mu_i, sigma_i) and the prediction weight is q_i = min(1.0, [kappa/sigma_i]^2). The abstention fraction is set explicitly or via a PID controller (e.g., tau = P_80% of validation sigma for 20% abstention); alpha = 0.1 works well and kappa = P_90% outperformed alternatives. The abstention loss outperforms the standard NLL-with-uncertainty approach on synthetic climate regression use cases.

For classification, the CAN 'NotWrong loss' is L_NW(x_j) = -log(p_j + p_{k+1}) - alpha log q, where p_{k+1} is the likelihood of an added abstention class and q = 1 - p_{k+1} = sum_{m=1}^k p_m is the likelihood of not abstaining; it focuses on getting the answer not wrong rather than right. It outperforms the baseline ANN and the DAC loss L_DAC(x_j) = -q log(p_j/q) - alpha log q on climate use cases, and for 40%-80% coverage the best CAN models reach accuracies similar to an ORACLE that knows which samples are corrupted.

A table-tennis stroke recognition dataset of 22,111 videos covering 11 basic strokes from 14 professional players was collected with a novel low-interference setup; a temporal convolutional network (TCN) on 2D human-pose estimation classifies the 11 strokes with 99.37% validation accuracy, and generalizes to a player excluded from training with 98.72% accuracy. Layer normalization improved TCN training; an HRNet/MPII-based variant only reached 82.36% validation accuracy.

Unsupervised contrastive learning trains a CNN embedding to cluster hockey players by team affiliation without labeled data or prior jersey knowledge; it reaches 94% team-classification accuracy after unsupervised training on a single frame and 97% within 500 frames (17 seconds of game time), substantially outperforming prior unsupervised approaches (colour histograms, bag-of-colours, autoencoders), and enables accurate team-conditional player-positioning heat maps. The paper also releases a new annotated hockey dataset.

Using only unsupervised techniques, random-forest regression selected variables predicting goal difference, Euclidean team distances were embedded with Laplacian eigenmaps, and bisecting the Fiedler vector revealed four natural clusters across the five major European football leagues from five metrics (shots, shots on target, shots conceded, possession, pass success); the top two clusters identify league-dominating teams as the best candidates for a competitive elite Super League.

From body-sensor traces of three professional football matches, a linear-interaction stochastic model for player motion: M_n ddot(vec(r))_n = -gamma_n vec(v)_n + k_an(vec(a)_n - vec(r)_n) + sum'_m k_nm(vec(r)_m - vec(r)_n), combining damping, an anchor to each player's position, and pairwise interaction forces (with separate horizontal/vertical 2-D diagonal parameter matrices). Measured statistics: mean relative ellipse area <s(t)> = 5.1 (sigma_s = 2.2), order parameter <phi(t)> = 0.7 (sigma_phi = 0.2), and return-time power-law exponents gamma_s = 0.96 +- 0.03 and gamma_phi = 2.16 +- 0.04 (vs 3/2 for a 1-D random-walk first return).

An automated rugby-union tackle injury-risk system chains YOLO ball detection with Kalman-filter tracking, a separate YOLO person detector to find ball-carrier and tackler within tackle segments, and OpenPose poses whose relative geometry evaluates tackle risk; on a diverse rugby tackle collection it achieved 62.50% evaluation accuracy. At a 15% high-risk region on n=64 evaluated tackles: accuracy 62.50%, recall 70.59%, precision 38.71%, F1 0.50; the 5% region gave highest overall accuracy while the 25% region gave highest high-risk accuracy (82.35%).

Sportlogiq's 'Detecting and Matching Related Objects with One Proposal Multiple Predictions' detects players and related objects (sticks, rackets, torsos) through the same proposal box with implicit association, trained with L_total = L_cls + L_loc^{base} + sum_{i=1}^n (L_loc^i + L_constraint^i) and a SetNMS procedure at inference to suppress duplicate detection sets in crowded scenes. On broadcast ice hockey, matching AP rose from 57.1% to 81.4% and player+stick mean AP from 68.4% to 88.3%; on the new public COCO+Torso dataset matching improved from 47.9% to 65.2%.

Szczecinski's 'Simplified Kalman filter for online rating: one-fits-all approach' is a generic Bayesian approximate-Kalman-filter framework for online sports rating that works with any skills-outcome model for individual or team sports; Elo, Glicko, and TrueSkill are shown to be instances of it, and numerical examples on synthetic and empirical data clarify when the Bayesian approach's gains over simpler solutions materialize.

The rating framework models the skills-outcome relationship as Pr{y_t | theta_t} = L(z_t/s; y_t) with z_t = x_{t,h}^T theta_t - x_{t,a}^T theta_t (home minus away skill combination), and binary outcomes via L(z;y) = F(z) if y = 1 (home win), F(-z) if y = 0 (away win), with F non-decreasing in [0,1]. Skill dynamics follow the damped random walk theta_t = beta_t theta_{t-1} + u_t epsilon_t, beta_t = beta^{(tau(t) - tau(t-1))}, and the Bayesian posterior is approximated by a Gaussian f-tilde(theta_t | y-bar_t) = N(theta_t; mu_t, V_t).

For large tournaments of software agents in asymmetric games, the Self-Consistent Elo (SC-Elo) update R = mu + beta sigma^2 (A - E(R)) is the posterior maximum-likelihood estimate that evaluates expected wins E(R) at the NEW rating R, whereas classic Elo R = mu + beta sigma^2 (A - E(mu)) evaluates at the OLD rating mu and suffers overshoot: as the number of games N grows, the adjustment mu + beta sigma^2 N (f - p-hat) grows without limit (over-extrapolation). E(R) is computed via Taylor expansion E(R) ~= E(mu) + s(R - mu) with slope s = dE/dr = beta sum_i p_i(r)(1 - p_i(r)).

Elo win probability is derived from strengths S = e^{beta R} with beta = ln(10)/400, giving P[A > B] = S_A/(S_A + S_B) = 1/(1 + e^{beta(R_B - R_A)}) = 1/(1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400}); Bayesian Elo starts from a Gaussian rating prior p[R] = e^{-(R-mu)^2/(2 sigma^2)}/(sqrt(2 pi) sigma) and posterior p[R|T] proportional to the product of win/loss likelihoods times the prior.

The Bristol Betting Exchange (BBE, Dave Cliff) is the first free open-source agent-based simulation of an in-play sports-betting exchange: it couples an exchange matching engine with a minimal race simulation (horse/car races on a 1-D track) and a population of bettors who each form private odds evaluations and bet before and during the race, updating opinions second-by-second. It is offered as a synthetic data generator (SDG) for AI/ML discovery of betting-exchange strategies, with race progress d_c(t+delta_t) = d_c(t) + S_c(t, f-vec_r) and factor-modulated steps S_c(t, f-vec_r) = (k - |f-vec_r - p-vec_c|) . U(d_min, d_max), plus blocking dynamics via Delta_c(t) = d_{i+}(t) - d_c(t) against a threshold theta_{c+}.

A system for tracking multiple soccer players across different video qualities adapts a state-of-the-art multiple-object-tracking method; the authors created detection and tracking datasets at three video-quality levels, and report conclusive high-performance tracking in low-quality video.

Ravi, Gokhale and Nagwekar propose three game-theoretic approaches for optimal strategy in two-player sports (badminton), with a normal-form game G = <I, (s_i)_{i in I}, (u_i)_{i in I}> and shot utility u_i(s_i, s_{-i}) = P(s_i|s_{-i}) * P_{success}(s_i|s_{-i}), where P is the probability of playing shot s_i against the opponent's shot s_{-i} and P_success is its success rate. The extensive-form version adds an RL-inspired reward: u_i(s_i,s_{-i}) = P(s_i|s_{-i}) * P_{success}(s_i|s_{-i}) * R_T(s_i,s_{-i}); the best response to an opponent shot is the player's shot maximizing this utility.

'Quantifying Uncertainty in Deep Spatiotemporal Forecasting' (KDD 2021) unifies Bayesian and frequentist uncertainty-quantification methods for spatiotemporal forecasting (grid- and graph-based) under statistical decision theory, tested on real road-network traffic, epidemics, and air-quality forecasting. Key findings: Bayesian methods are typically more robust in mean prediction, while frequentist confidence levels give more extensive coverage over data variation; quantile-regression methods are computationally cheaper for a single interval but must be retrained for different intervals, whereas sampling methods generate samples usable for multiple intervals at higher cost. They train deep nets with the Mean Interval Score (MIS) loss, whose minimizers yield (1-rho)-confidence intervals, and with quantile loss L_Quantile(y, f(x); theta, rho) = min_theta E_{(x,y)~D}[(y - f(x))(rho - 1{y < f(x)})].

In 'Ranking earthquake forecasts using proper scoring rules', the Parimutuel Gambling score used by CSEP experiments is proved analytically to be in general improper: on average it does not prefer the data-generating model even when that model is known. With p-bar = sum_{i=1}^k p_i / k, the score is S_{G,i}(p|x) = p_i/p-bar - 1 when x = 1 and (1 - p_i)/(1 - p-bar) - 1 when x = 0; it is zero-sum (sum_i S_{G,i}(p|x) = 0) and its bias direction depends on which forecasts participate. For two forecasts with p_2 = p* (the truth), S^E_{G,1}(p|p*) >= S^E_{G,2}(p|p*) when p_1 is closer to p* than p_2, yet p_1 = p* does NOT maximize the expected score; conclusion: the Parimutuel Gambling score should not be used to distinguish multiple competing forecasts, and care is needed even for two. The positively oriented Brier score is S_B(P|x) = -sum_{z in X} [p(z) - I(z = x)]^2, and a rule is strictly proper iff E_X[Delta] = 0 iff p = p*, i.e., only the true model achieves the highest average score.

DeepMind's 'From Motor Control to Team Play in Simulated Humanoid Football' trains teams of physically simulated humanoid avatars to play football by combining imitation learning, single- and multi-agent reinforcement learning, and population-based training in stages: first realistic human-like locomotion (running, turning), then mid-level skills (dribbling, shooting), then team awareness — bridging low-level motor control at millisecond timescales to coordinated goal-directed team behavior over tens of seconds. The policy objective is F^k(pi) := E[sum_{t=1}^T r^k_i(s_t)] over dynamics and coplayer sampling, and the surrogate objective for agent parameters theta is J^k(theta; theta^h) := E[sum_{ell=1}^{M_k} alpha_{k,ell} sum_{t=0}^inf gamma_{k,ell}^t r-hat_i^{(k,ell)}(s_{tau+t})].

Pelechrinis' 'The Anatomy of Corner 3s in the NBA' uses player-tracking data to show the main factor behind corner-three efficiency is NOT the shorter distance to the basket versus above-the-break threes, but that corner threes are assisted at a very high rate (more than 90%). More than half involve a shooter anchored at the corner waiting for the kick-out pass. A simplified offense-vs-defense game yields a Nash equilibrium supporting either fully committing to the corner shooter or fully committing to the drive — not lingering between the two, which is what defenses were actually observed doing.

Barrett, Koumarianos and Mermut present 'How a losing team like the Canadiens can steal a Stanley Cup: A quantitative intransitive hockey analysis,' a simple mathematical model claimed to provide a successful strategy for ending Canadian Hockey Teams' championship futility (only title and abstract were recoverable from this document).

'The Evaluation of Rating Systems in Team-based' games compares Elo, Glicko, and TrueSkill evaluation metrics on over 25,000 team battle-royale matches: some metrics were highly impacted by the inclusion of new players and many could not capture real differences between player groups, but normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG) demonstrated more reliable performance and more flexibility, alleviating most challenges faced by the other metrics while allowing evaluators to adjust focus on different player groups. NDCG = (sum_{i=1}^N (1/log_2(i+1)) * (1/(1+error_i))) / IDCG, where error_i is the absolute difference between predicted and observed rank of team t_i.

For Elo adapted to team battle-royale games, a team rating is the sum of member ratings mu_{t_i} = sum_{j=1}^n mu_j; win probability averages pairwise logistic probabilities Pr(t_i wins, F) = (sum_{1<=j<=N, i!=j} (1 + e^{(mu_{t_j} - mu_{t_i})/D})^{-1}) / C(N,2); observed rank is normalized as R'_{t_i} = (N - R^{obs}_{t_i}) / C(N,2); team rating updates as mu'_{t_i} = mu_{t_i} + K[R'_{t_i} - Pr(t_i wins, F)], and individual player ratings receive contribution-weighted shares mu'_j = mu_j + w_{p_j}(mu'_{t_i} - mu_{t_i}) with w_{p_j} = mu_j / mu_{t_i}. TrueSkill's non-draw update is mu'_i = mu_i + (sigma_i^2/c)[N(t/c)/Phi(t/c)] with t = mu_i - mu_j and c = sqrt(2 beta^2 + sigma_i^2 + sigma_j^2).

'Enhancing Trajectory Prediction' on soccer data found it surprisingly challenging to train deep models that beat linear extrapolation on average predicted-vs-true trajectory distance: simple MLPs and RNNs generally cannot convincingly outperform linear extrapolation with conventional training. Predicting a sparse trajectory and interpolating with constant acceleration improves L2 error for several models, and applying the same sparse-subset + interpolation post hoc monotonically improves L2 with sparsity up to 4 seconds between outputs for all tested models. Conditioning defender predictions on the full trajectories of other players (ball/attackers) dramatically improves L2, further improved with sparse predictions. The GraN-MA architecture (graph networks + multi-head attention) outperformed state-of-the-art RED and GVRNN on their dataset. The constant-acceleration interpolation derives from s_t = v_0 t + a t^2/2, giving a = 2(s_T - v_0 T)/T^2.

'Learning Football Body-Orientation as a Matter of Classification' (Arbues Sanguesa et al.) is the first deep-learning model estimating football player orientation directly from video footage, framed as classification over orientation bins with a cyclic loss; it trains on ground truth from wearable EPTS devices compensated for camera pose via alpha_i = alpha'_i - angle(F_i F_i^0 vector). Soft ground-truth labels follow y_{ij} = exp(-phi(alpha_i, r_j)) / sum_{k=1}^K exp(-phi(alpha_i, r_k)), where phi(alpha_i, r_j) = min(|alpha_i - r_j|, 360 - |alpha_i - r_j|)^2/90 is cyclic distance to bin center r_j. It achieved median absolute deviation error of 11.60 degrees on the test set, beating the previous computer-vision state of the art (28 degrees) by more than 20 degrees.

'What Happened Next?' introduces DAxT (Defensive Action Expected Threat), a deep-learning metric valuing defensive actions (tackles, interceptions) by studying the threat of the passages of play they prevented, validated on 2017/2018 and 2018/2019 English Premier League event data, with model outputs combined with additional features into an overall defensive-ability rating for players. It builds on Expected Threat xT_{x,y} = (s_{x,y} x g_{x,y}) + (m_{x,y} x sum_{z=1}^{16} sum_{w=1}^{12} T_{(x,y)->(z,w)} xT_{z,w}), where s_{x,y} is the probability of shooting from position (x,y), g_{x,y} the probability that shot scores (xG), m_{x,y} the move probability, and T the transition matrix.

Boffi et al.'s 'Nonparametric adaptive control and prediction' drops the standard assumption that system uncertainty lies in the linear span of known basis functions: they introduce a nonparametric adaptive algorithm that estimates an infinite-dimensional density over parameters online to learn unknown dynamics in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, whose control input surprisingly admits an analytical expression. A randomized implementation via random Fourier features recovers classical parametric complexity while provably retaining nonparametric expressivity, with explicit bounds depending only polynomially on system parameters, and the method learned a predictive model of a 60-dimensional system of ten point masses interacting through Newtonian gravitation. Extended to deep neural networks via reinterpretation as gradient flow, extra deep-representation expressivity empirically improved performance at the expense of the closed-loop stability that kernel machines rigorously guarantee.

'Deep Learning Statistical Arbitrage' builds a unifying conceptual framework and data-driven ML solution: asset returns follow a conditional factor model R_{n,t} = beta_{n,t-1}^T F_t + epsilon_{n,t} with arbitrage portfolios defined as residuals epsilon_{n,t} = R_{n,t} - beta_{n,t-1}^T F_t (unconditional mean zero), and allocation functions are optimized over expected utility / Sharpe ratio subject to leverage normalization w^R_{t-1} = (w^eps_{t-1})^T Phi_{t-1} / ||(w^eps_{t-1})^T Phi_{t-1}||_1. Residuals are modeled as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes dX_t = kappa(mu - X_t)dt + sigma dB_t with signal theta^OU = (kappa-hat, mu-hat, sigma-hat, X_L, R^2), and the classic threshold rule goes long/short when |X_L - mu|/(sigma/sqrt(2 kappa)) > c_thresh with R^2 > c_crit. The authors report consistently high out-of-sample mean returns and Sharpe ratios substantially outperforming all benchmarks.

Gilch's 'UEFA EURO 2020 Forecast via Nested Zero-Inflated Generalized Poisson Regression' forecasts EURO 2020 (played June/July 2021) with a zero-inflated generalized Poisson model: P[X=k] = omega + (1-omega)e^{-mu/varphi} for k=0 and (1-omega) mu (mu+(varphi-1)k)^{k-1}/(k!) varphi^{-k} e^{-(mu+(varphi-1)k)/varphi} for k>=1, with E(X)=(1-omega)mu and Var(X)=(1-omega)mu(varphi^2+omega mu). The location covariate is loc_{A|B} = 1 if A at home, 0 if neutral, -1 if B at home. The nested structure models team A's goals from opponent B's Elo and location, log mu_A(Elo_B) = alpha_0^{(1)} + alpha_1^{(1)} Elo_B + alpha_2^{(1)} loc_{A|B}, and goals B receives against higher-Elo teams, then averages them: mu_{A|B} = (mu_A(Elo_B) + nu_B(Elo_A))/2 (with varphi and omega averaged likewise); the second team's goals are then modeled conditional on G_A. Monte Carlo simulation of each match then the whole tournament; fitted on all participating teams' games since 2014 weighted by date and importance. Example: France's expected goals against Germany = 1.627 (France mu=1.35521, omega=0.044888; Germany nu=1.988806, delta=0.003993638).

'Evaluating Team Skill Aggregation in Online Competitive Games' (Dehpanah & Ghori) addresses how team skill is computed from member skills — an under-studied step in rating systems — proposing two new aggregation methods alongside the standard SUM approach and exhaustively comparing them with Elo, Glicko, and TrueSkill on over 100,000 battle-royale and head-to-head matches. The MAX method (a team's performance determined by its most skilled member) was superior in the majority of tested cases, implying team performance is best determined by the most skilled member; the authors call for more elaborate aggregation methods covering skills, strategy, and goals.

Foulley's 'More on verification of probability forecasts for football outcomes' adds score decompositions (Brier, Ranked Probability, Logarithmic, Zero-One) plus reliability, resolution, and discrimination analyses via several binning techniques (fixed thresholds, quantiles, logistic, isotonic regression), illustrated on four seasons of UEFA Champions League group-stage outcomes using Poisson regression models versus bookmaker-odds forecasts. Reliability is assessed with Cox's model logit[Pr(X_i = 1)] = alpha + beta logit(p_i), where alpha = 0, beta = 1 is perfect reliability. Results: Poisson models show reasonably good reliability and resolution versus bookmaker odds; home wins are over-forecasted (alpha-hat = -0.26, beta-hat = 1.11, P = 0.03 and 0.38), away wins are very well calibrated (alpha-hat = 0.076, beta-hat = 1.053), and draws lack forecasting resolution and discrimination. The bivariate Poisson uses y_ij^{(t),k} | lambda_ij^{(t,k)} ~ P(lambda_ij^{(t,k)}) with log lambda_ij^{(t,1)} = eta + h + beta_1 Delta r_ij(t') + beta_2 r-bar_ij(t') and log lambda_ij^{(t,2)} = eta + beta_1 Delta r_ji(t') + beta_2 r-bar_ij(t'), and automatically generates a negative home-away goal correlation (rho_12 = -0.19 versus observed -0.24 +/- 0.16, 95% CI).

'Poisoning Attack against Estimating from Pairwise Comparisons' (K. Ma) initiates the first systematic investigation of data poisoning attacks on pairwise ranking algorithms: the ranker-vs-attacker interaction is formalized as dynamic and static games and as integer programming problems, reformulated into computationally tractable distributionally robust optimization (DRO) problems, yielding two efficient poisoning attack algorithms with theoretical guarantees including Nash equilibrium existence and generalization bounds. Simulations and real-data experiments show the attacks significantly degrade the ranker: the correlation between the true ranking list and the results aggregated with toxic data decreases dramatically. The rank-estimation loss is the weighted sum of squares l(theta; C_U) = (1/(2|C_U|)) sum_{(i,j)} w^0_{ij} (y_{ij} - theta_i + theta_j)^2, with attacker actions constrained by l1/infinity budgets on weight perturbations.

ggViz is a visual analytics system that lets users query large CSGO esports datasets through hand-drawn game-state sketches to find similar game states: a performant tokenization summarizes states and the retrieval R(N, S, q) = {s_1, ..., s_n} returns all states s_i with token T(s_i) = T(q) for query q over navigation mesh N and state set S. It achieves interactive performance across 10+ million game states and was evaluated with coaches, managers, and analysts from professional esports teams; e.g., a 2v3 retake situation showed position S1 at 12% win rate versus S2 (5%) and S3 (0%).

This paper proposes combining Item Response Theory (IRT) with rating systems to summarize results across datasets into robust ML benchmarks: the Glicko system improves on Elo by accounting for players' activity periods, and IRT is suggested for improving classifiers, creating algorithm portfolios, classifier selection, understanding dataset complexity, and assessing classifiers with IRT. The 3-parameter logistic IRT model gives the probability of individual j answering item i correctly as P(U_ij=1|theta_j) = c_i + (1-c_i)/(1+e^{-a_i(theta_j - b_i)}), where theta_j is ability, b_i item difficulty, a_i discrimination, and c_i the guessing parameter; the adversary method is used to iteratively create state-of-the-art models and non-aging benchmarks.

Piancastelli's 'Multivariate Conway-Maxwell-Poisson Distribution: Sarmanov Method and Doubly-Intractable Bayesian Inference' proposes the MultCOMP model with COM-Poisson marginals p(x|lambda,nu) = lambda^x/((x!)^nu Z(lambda,nu)), Z(lambda,nu) = sum_{x=0}^inf lambda^x/(x!)^nu, admitting a flexible covariance matrix with both negative and positive off-diagonals (unlike existing bivariate COM-Poisson constructions which lack COM-Poisson marginals). The bivariate Sarmanov construction is f(x_1,x_2) = f_1(x_1)f_2(x_2){1 + delta phi_1(x_1)phi_2(x_2)}, extended to d dimensions as f(x_1,...,x_d) = {prod_{i=1}^d f_i(x_i)} {C(d,2) + sum_{j<k} delta_{jk} phi_j(x_j) phi_k(x_k)}/C(d,2). The doubly-intractable posterior is handled via the exchange algorithm and Grouped Independence Metropolis-Hastings. Applied to Premier League home/away goal counts 2018–2021, the model shows evidence of a decreased number of goals scored by the home team (not accompanied by reduced away scoring) during the crowdless COVID period, i.e., a smaller home-team advantage in the absence of crowds.

'The reaction to news in live betting' (Oetting, Michels, Langrock, Deutscher) uses a high-resolution 1 Hz dataset from a large European bookmaker to study how live football betting markets respond to news, modeling stakes with a zero-adjusted gamma (ZAGA) distribution y_t ~ ZAGA(mu_t, sigma, pi_t) with f(y_t) = pi_t if y_t = 0 else (1 - pi_t) h(y_t), in a state-space framework where the market activity state g_t = phi g_{t-1} + beta_1 halftime_t + beta_2 ginidiff_t + sum_{j=3}^{5} beta_j 1/goalteam^{(j)}_t + sigma_g eta_t (j = 3 surprising, j = 4 slightly, j = 5 unsurprising goals), mu_t = exp(alpha_0 + covariates + g_t), and the zero-stake probability pi_t = logit^{-1}(gamma_0 + gamma_1 gini_t + gamma_2 gini_t^2 + gamma_3 int_t + gamma_4 gini_t int_t + gamma_5 gini_t^2 int_t) when the market is open. The results indicate markets might overreact to recent news, confirming cognitive biases known from psychology and behavioral economics.

Gneiting and Resin's 'Regression Diagnostics meets Forecast Evaluation' develops a probability-theoretic framework giving hierarchies of calibration for real-valued outcomes, applying to both predictive distributions and stand-alone point forecasts: a prediction is conditionally T-calibrated if it can be taken at face value in terms of the functional T (threshold exceedance, quantiles, expectiles, moments via identification functions), and auto-calibration is the strongest notion (AC implies STC/TC/QC/CC in the calibration hierarchy). They introduce population T-reliability diagrams and revisit the score decomposition into miscalibration (MCB), discrimination (DSC), and uncertainty (UNC), with stable estimators via nonparametric isotonic regression and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm. For in-sample diagnostics they propose the universal coefficient of determination R* = (DSC - MCB)/UNC, which nests classical R^2 in least-squares mean regression and R^1 in quantile regression while applying to T-regression generally (MCB >= 0, DSC >= 0, R* in [0,1] under modest conditions).

A Vietnamese-language methods paper titled (translated) 'Modeling the number of goals per match by the home team in the Premier League using generalized linear regression with a Poisson-distributed dependent variable'; the extractable content was limited to the title (no equations or claims recovered from this document).

Kipf et al.'s 'Neural Relational Inference for Interacting Systems' (ICML) is an unsupervised model that simultaneously infers interactions and learns dynamics purely from observational data, in the form of a variational auto-encoder whose latent code represents the underlying interaction graph and whose reconstruction decoder is based on graph neural networks. The NRI model recovered ground-truth interaction graphs with high accuracy on simulated physical systems (on par with a supervised gold standard on springs), learned a small number of interpretable edge types on real motion-capture and NBA basketball data (including pick-and-roll structure), and beat LSTM baselines. A noted limitation: when interactions have only small effects on short-term dynamics, the optimizer can settle on a sub-optimal decoder that ignores the latent edges at only marginally worse reconstruction loss. Training objective is the ELBO L = E_{q_phi(z|x)}[log p_theta(x|z)] - KL[q_phi(z|x) || p_theta(z)], with autoregressive decoder p_theta(x|z) = prod_{t=1}^T p_theta(x^{t+1} | x^t, ..., x^1, z) and edge updates H^1_e = f_e([M^{in}_{v->e} H^1_v, M^{out}_{v->e} H^1_v]).

PlayeRank (Pappalardo et al.) is a data-driven framework for multi-dimensional, role-aware evaluation of soccer player performance and ranking: it computes a performance rating per player per match from soccer-log events and aggregates over sequences of matches, built on millions of match events across four seasons of 18 prominent competitions. Compared against known soccer performance-evaluation algorithms and validated against professional soccer scouts' evaluations, PlayeRank significantly outperforms the competitors; its rating patterns reveal what distinguishes top players, and applications include player search and player versatility.

Alexandari, Kundaje and Shrikumar present a general abstention (selective classification) framework that can optimize any metric of interest rather than only top-k accuracy — with computationally efficient algorithms for sensitivity at a target specificity, auROC, and weighted Cohen's Kappa — while adapting to label shift (changed class proportions between training and test time) and working out-of-the-box with any calibrated classifier. The key idea: calibrated probability estimates serve as a proxy for true class labels, allowing estimation of the change in an arbitrary metric if an example were abstained on; they also introduce a novel strong baseline based on JS divergence from prior class probabilities. Experiments on synthetic, biological, and clinical data support the findings; e.g., on a 1:9 positive:negative dataset, optimal abstention boundaries differ dramatically between optimizing auROC, sensitivity at 90% specificity, and accuracy.

Blanco, Salmeron and Gomez-Haro describe a multicriteria outranking methodology to rank sports players by efficiency: alternatives are the players, criteria are different efficiency indices (points, playing time, tries, etc.), with a novel automatic parameter-tuning approach letting coaches and sports managers design templates and strategies; the case study runs it on the Spanish ACB Basketball League and is designed to be implemented and interpreted by decision-makers unfamiliar with the mathematics.

Babichenko and Garber's 'Learning of Optimal Forecast Aggregation in Partial Evidence Environments' considers repeated binary-event forecasting where Bayesian honest experts share a common prior but observe different subsets of conditionally independent signals, while the aggregator observes only the forecasts (not the evidence or information structure) and sees the realized state each period. Main result: optimal aggregation — the Bayesian aggregation of ALL signals in the system, a much stronger benchmark than the best expert — can be learned in polynomial time across a wide range of partial-evidence instances, with a tight characterization of where learning is possible versus impossible. Accuracy is measured by proper scoring rules, focusing on logarithmic loss.

'Model Trees for Identifying Exceptional Players in the NHL Draft' combines model-based and cohort-based approaches: a model tree partitions the feature space on discrete features or learned thresholds of continuous features, each leaf defines an interpretable group of comparable players (discovered from data without a similarity metric) with its own group regression model, forming an ensemble more powerful than a single model. Predictions are competitive with state-of-the-art methods and case studies show the ranking adds information to the NHL Central Scouting Service Rank; out-of-sample Pearson correlations of predicted ranks with future NHL success were 0.69, 0.72, 0.60, 0.58 for the tree model versus 0.43, 0.45, 0.48, 0.51 for raw draft order across the tested draft-year windows. The LogitBoost variant combines a model tree with weighted votes, fitting separate models at every node (not just leaves) for hierarchical-shrinkage-like smoothing.

Egidi et al.'s 'bookmakers' odds in modelling football scores' builds a hierarchical Bayesian Poisson model in which team scoring rates are convex combinations of parameters estimated from historical data and from betting odds: gamma-hat_{m1} = p-hat_{m1} theta-hat_{m1} + (1 - p-hat_{m1}) lambda-hat_{m1}, and the goal difference Y_{m1} - Y_{m2} follows a Poisson-difference (Skellam) distribution PD(gamma-hat_{m1}, gamma-hat_{m2}). Win/draw probabilities come from pi_{Win,m} + pi_{Draw,m} = P(y_{m1} >= y_{m2} | theta_{m1}, theta_{m2}), and predictions use the posterior predictive p(y-tilde|y) = integral p(theta|y) p(y-tilde|theta) d theta. Fitted on nine years of data from the most popular European leagues to predict match outcomes of their tenth seasons, with numerical and graphical model checks.

'The Advantage of Doubling' analyzes NBA double-teaming with deep reinforcement learning on player trajectory data from over 643,000 possessions: the learned policy value estimates of defensive actions are predictive of points per possession and win percentage. Findings: doubling significantly lowers the offense's field goal percentage but at the expense of a significantly greater likelihood of the possession ending in a foul; observed and learned doubling policies differ significantly, and under 'optimal' play all teams could improve their defense. The Q-network loss is L = sum sum [Q^pi(s_t^i, a_t^i) - (r_t^i + V^pi(s_{t+1}^i))]^2 with double Q-learning and a periodically cached target network for stability.

AURORA (Kang et al.) formally defines the PageRank auditing problem: instead of asking which nodes are most important, identify the set of key graph elements (edges, nodes, subgraphs) with the highest influence on PageRank ranking results, formulated as an optimization problem. The Aurora family of algorithms measures influence of graph elements via gradients w.r.t. the ranking results and incrementally selects the most influential ones; node influence enjoys the diminishing-returns property, justifying a greedy algorithm, and the methods scale linearly to large graphs while outperforming baselines on real-world datasets.

Koch's 'Spatial risk measures and rate of spatial diversification' defines a spatial risk measure as the application of a classical risk measure Pi (expectation, variance, Value-at-Risk, expected shortfall) to the normalized integral of a cost random field C over geographical areas, plus axioms describing how risk evolves with the space variable — notably asymptotic spatial homogeneity, whose order quantifies the rate of spatial diversification as the region grows. For a general cost field (and also when the cost field is a function of a max-stable random field, the natural model for spatially-extended extreme events), sufficient conditions are given so that the spatial risk measures associated with expectation, variance, VaR, and expected shortfall satisfy asymptotic spatial homogeneity of order 0, -2, -1, and -1 respectively.

Garcia et al.'s 'Structured Output Learning with Abstention (SOLA)' lets a structured-output model abstain from predicting some labels at a user-chosen cost: the problem is decomposed into learning a pair of predictors (one for structured abstention, one for structured prediction), compared via a wide class of asymmetric abstention-aware losses based on embeddings of desired and abstention-containing outputs in the same space. Learning uses surrogate least-squares regression in a feature space and prediction solves a new pre-image problem, with statistical guarantees on excess risk. Applied to fine-grained opinion mining it gives state-of-the-art results, and its abstention-aware sentence-level opinion representations competitively predict user-review ratings.

'Fine-grained Activity Recognition in Baseball Videos' introduces the MLB-YouTube dataset with densely annotated broadcast baseball frames for segmented video classification and continuous activity detection. Findings: learning temporal structure is valuable — temporal convolution beats mean/max pooling, fixed temporal pyramids, and LSTMs (which overfit small pitch-type differences); learning important sub-event intervals for pooling helps, and combining the convolutional sub-event representation with a super-event representation gives the best performance. On pitch-type classification: fastballs easiest (68% accuracy), sliders 45%, sinkers hardest (12%).

Passi and Pandey predict cricket player performance (batsman runs and bowler wickets as classification problems) using Naive Bayes, Random Forest, multiclass SVM, and decision trees. Random Forest was the most accurate for both problems: 90.74% accuracy predicting runs and 92.25% predicting wickets with 90% training data; Naive Bayes was worst (42.5% for runs, 57.05% for wickets at 90% training). Model accuracy rises with training-set size for all algorithms except Naive Bayes on batting.

twAwler is a lightweight Twitter crawler targeting language-specific communities that exploits multiple Twitter API endpoints to explore user relations while respecting all policies and rate limits.
