Elo ratings are systematically biased even at stationarity: for X~pi typically E[X]!=rho, i.e. the stationary mean does not equal the vector of true skills even though the process is mean-preserving per game.

One Elo update is a contraction in the coupled norm: with Delta_ij=b(x^i-x^j)-b(y^i-y^j) the i-th coordinate changes as (E^i_alpha(x)-E^i_alpha(y))^2=(x^i-y^i)^2-2K(x^i-y^i)Delta_ij+K^2 Delta_ij^2, and the distance ||X_t-Y_t|| between two coupled rating trajectories is non-increasing a.s. with limit 0.
Stability of Elo is proved with the Lyapunov function V(x)=sum_i cosh(a(x^i-rho^i)): E[V(X_1)|X_0=x]-V(x)<=-cV(x)+c-tilde, a geometric drift toward a compact set uniformly in the ratings.

Mean Per-Joint Position Error is MPJPE=(1/N)sum_i||p_i-p-hat_i||_2, and its Procrustes-aligned variant is PA-MPJPE=(1/N)sum_i||p_i - s R p-hat_i - t||_2 with optimal scale s, rotation R and translation t removing rigid misalignment before error measurement.

EITNet's detection head uses BiFPN feature fusion features=sum_i alpha_i*F_i with attention-normalized fusion Attention BiFPN=F_current/(F_previous+epsilon), bounding-box regression from anchors through a sigmoid, and total loss Loss_total=Loss_cls+lambda*Loss_reg; accuracy is (correct predictions)/(total predictions)x100%.
equation: \text{Loss}_{\text{total}}=\text{Loss}_{\text{cls}}+\lambda\cdot\text{Loss}_{\text{reg}},\quad \text{Accuracy}=\frac{\text{Number of Correct Predictions}}{\text{Total Number of Predictions}}\times 100\%

claim: EITNet (EfficientDet + I3D + TimeSformer with IoT data pipeline) reaches 92% basketball action recognition accuracy versus the EfficientDet baseline's 87%, with training loss below 5.0 versus 9.0 over 50 epochs; ablations show accuracy drops when I3D or TimeSformer is removed (47.6/40.9 without I3D, 46.8/39.7 without TimeSformer on the reported metrics).

The confidence-based reject-option classifier is h(f(x),rho)=1{f(x)>rho}+perp*1{|f(x)|<=rho}-1{f(x)<-rho} (predict +1, abstain, or -1); its loss is l_d(yf(x),rho)=1{yf(x)<=-rho}+d*1{|f(x)|<=rho} with rejection cost d, and the Bayes optimal is f*_d(x)=1{eta>1-d}+perp*1{d<=eta<=1-d}-1{eta<d} where eta=P(Y=1|x).

The adversarially robust reject-option loss takes worst-case perturbations in an L2 ball of radius gamma: l_d^gamma(yf(x),rho)=(1-d)*sup_{||x-x'||_2<=gamma}1{yf(x')<-rho}+d*sup_{||x-x'||_2<=gamma}1{yf(x')<=rho}; for linear classifiers H_lin={x->w.x: ||w||=1} this collapses to (1-d)1{yf(x)<-rho+gamma}+d*1{yf(x)<=rho+gamma}.

A surrogate l2 is (l1,H)-calibrated iff excess l2-risk vanishing implies excess l1-risk vanishing: R_{l2}(f_n)-R*_{l2,H}->0 => R_{l1}(f_n)-R*_{l1,H}->0, with uniform calibration function delta(epsilon)=inf_{eta,f,x}{C_{l2,H}(f(x),eta)-C*_{l2,H}(x,eta) | C_{l1,H}(f(x),eta)-C*_{l1,H}(x,eta)>=epsilon}; calibration holds iff delta(epsilon)>0 for all epsilon>0.

Negative calibration result: convex surrogates and quasi-concave conditional-risk surrogates, which are calibrated in the adversarial setting without a reject option, are NOT calibrated for the adversarial robust reject-option loss l_d^gamma; the paper gives a complete characterization of which surrogates are (l_d^gamma,H_lin)-calibrated and shows empirically that Shifted Double Ramp Loss and Shifted Double Sigmoid Loss satisfy the conditions and resist adversarial perturbations on synthetic data.
GlickFormer standardizes puzzle difficulty labels as mu_i=(r_i-1516)/543 and phi_i=RD_i/543, treating the Glicko-2 rating and its rating deviation as an uncertain regression target.

Puzzle-difficulty metrics: MSE loss L=(1/M)sum_i(y-hat_i-y_i)^2; MAE=(1/N)sum_i|r_i-r-hat_i|; MAZ=(1/N)sum_i|(r_i-r-hat_i)/RD_i| (error in units of rating deviation); accuracy within kRD=(1/N)sum_i I(|r_i-r-hat_i|<=k*RD_i) for k=1,2,3.

GlickFormer predicts chess puzzle difficulty with a transformer approximating the Glicko-2 system: boards encoded as B_n in R^{16x8x8}, a modified ChessFormer backbone for spatial features plus factorized temporal attention over move sequences, output y-hat=f(s_1^{(L_t)}); trained on 4M+ puzzles it beats the ChessFormer baseline and placed competitively in the IEEE BigData Cup 2024 puzzle-difficulty competition.

An e-process is a nonnegative adapted process with sup_{P in H} sup_tau E_P[E_tau]<=1; the anytime-valid test T_t(E,delta)=1[E_t>=1/delta] then satisfies P_P(exists t: E_t>=1/delta)<=delta under the null, giving sequential error control at any stopping time.

The nonparametric betting e-process for testing arm a's mean against threshold xi is E^a_t(lambda,xi)=prod_{i:A_i=a}(1+lambda(X_i-xi)); the predictable plug-in choice uses lambda^-_{t,a}=min(b/xi, max((mu-hat_{t-1}(a)-xi)/(xi(1-xi)),0)) for the bad-arm null and a mirrored lambda^+ for the good-arm null, where mu-hat is the running arm mean.

Minimax optimal e-power: for any e-process against the composite null H^-_a={P(mu_a): mu_a<=xi}, the worst-case normalized expected log-wealth inf_P sup_E E[log E_t]/N_t(a) equals log((1-mu_a)/(1-xi))+mu_a log(mu_a(1-xi)/(xi(1-mu_a))), achieved by the paper's plug-in e-process.

Good-arm identification with delta-level error control means P(exists tau_a: {G_t not subset of G_mu} union {B_t not subset of B_mu})<=delta, i.e. no arm is ever mislabeled with probability at least 1-delta; pairing regret-minimizing sampling with the anytime-valid test gives minimax optimal stopping times, cutting expected samples by at least 50% across synthetic and real settings.

Conformal Predictive Portfolio Selection: for portfolio w the return is R_{T+1}(w)=sum_a w_{a,T+1} Y_{a,T+1}; a conformal prediction interval C-hat^w_T(X_{T+1}) satisfies P(R_{T+1}(w) in C-hat^w_T(X_{T+1}))>=1-alpha, and portfolios are selected by a prediction-interval (PI) rule w-hat=PI({C-hat^w_T}_w).

The conformal p-value over block permutations Pi is p-hat(r)=(1/|Pi|)sum_{pi in Pi} 1[S(D^pi_{(r)})>=S(D_{(r)})] with nonconformity score S(D_{(r)})=1/(T+1)sum_{t=1}^{T+1}(R-tilde_t - f_T(X_t))^2, the mean squared residual of the predictive model f_T.

The highest-return-lowest-risk (HR-LR) rule keeps portfolios whose interval lower bound r-underbar^{w,alpha}_{T+1}=min C-hat^w_T is high (low risk) and picks w^{HR-LR}=argmax_{w in W-underbar} r-bar^{w,alpha}_{T+1} with r-bar=max C-hat^w_T (highest upside); CPPS with AR models and neural networks delivered superior returns to simpler strategies in empirical studies.

TranSPORTmer's masked multi-head attention is softmax(((QK^T)+o(M))/sqrt(d_k))V with binary mask M in {0,1}^{n x n_v} hiding missing or future observations, applied in Set Attention Blocks that are equivariant over agents while capturing temporal and social interactions.

TranSPORTmer trains the joint objective L=L_ADE+lambda L_CE where the state-classification loss is cross-entropy over 4 game states (pass, possession, uncontrolled, out-of-play): L_CE=-(1/T)sum_t sum_{c=1}^4 s^c_t log(s-hat^c_t).

Trajectory metrics: MaxErr=(1/D)sum_n max_t(||x^n_t-x-hat^n_t||_2 * M^n_t) with D=sum_n 1(sum_t M^n_t) the count of observed agents, capturing worst-case per-agent deviation; state accuracy Acc=(1/T)sum_t I(argmax_c s^c_t=argmax_c s-hat^c_t).

TranSPORTmer is a single unified transformer for multi-agent sports trajectory tasks (player forecasting, forecasting-imputation, ball inference, ball imputation, plus state classification via a CLS extra agent), outperforming state-of-the-art task-specific models on soccer and basketball datasets.

Systematic review finding: machine learning (support vector machines, random forests, neural networks) is applied across soccer, basketball, tennis and cricket for outcome prediction from historical, in-game and real-time data, dynamic odds-setting and risk management for bookmakers, and anomaly-detection-based fraud detection for suspicious patterns.

The review identifies open challenges in ML for sports betting: data quality, real-time decision-making, the inherent unpredictability of sports outcomes, and ethical concerns around transparency and fairness; future directions are adaptive models integrating multimodal data and portfolio-style risk management.

A precise scoring rule s: Delta^k x Omega -> R is weakly proper iff E_P[s(P,omega)]<=E_P[s(Q,omega)] for all P,Q in Delta^k; the paper generalizes proper scoring rules and calibration to imprecise (set-valued) forecasts Q(x) in IP, the nonempty subsets of the simplex.

Under imprecision the agent acts by MinMax: a*_{Q(x)}=argmin_{a in A} sup_{Q in Q(x)} E_Q[l(a,omega)], and the induced IP scoring rule is S-tilde_l(omega)=l(a*_{Q(X(omega))},omega); the optimal IP score is IP-Score*(l,P)=min_{Q:X->IP} sup_{P in P} E_P[S_l(Q(X(omega)),omega)].

The generalized conditional entropy is H_l(P|X)=E_P[S_l(P(.|X),omega)]; the max-entropy distribution P* in argmax_{P in co-bar(P)} H_l(P|X) drives optimal imprecise forecasting, and decision-theoretic entropy is the key object for both scoring-rule and calibration goals.

Key theoretical finding: proper scoring rules and calibration serve two distinct goals that are aligned for precise forecasts but not necessarily aligned for imprecise forecasts; the framework links imprecision to (group) distributional robustness and exposes subtle pitfalls in loss-function choice for distributional robustness.

Contact-implicit trajectory optimization encodes rigid contact with complementarity constraints c_i*beta_i(x_i,x_cs)=0, beta_i>=0, c_i>=0, where c_i is the contact force magnitude and beta_i the signed distance to the contact surface; friction stays inside the cone ||alpha_i||_2<=mu*c_i with mu the friction coefficient.

Polyhedral Coulomb friction is written as a linear complementarity system: lambda*e+D^T v perpendicular to alpha, lambda*e+D^T v>=0, alpha>=0, and (mu*c_i-e^T alpha) perpendicular to lambda, mu*c_i-e^T alpha>=0, lambda>=0, with D=[nu_1,...,nu_m] the tangential direction matrix.

DisCo's ADMM consensus couples single-robot subproblems through agreement constraints f_i=f_j for all neighbors j in N_i on contact forces (and on object states x-ring_i=x-ring_j); the augmented Lagrangian adds dual terms phi_ij^T(f_i-a_ij) and quadratic penalties 1/2||f_i-a_ij||^2_{W_f} summed over the neighborhood graph.
Inelastic robot-object impacts use the velocity-level complementarity c_i*(beta-dot_i(t+Delta t)+theta*beta-dot_i(t))=0 with coefficient of restitution theta=0 for perfectly inelastic collisions.

DisCo is a distributed contact-implicit trajectory optimization algorithm built on an ADMM variant: each robot solves its own smaller single-robot contact-implicit trajectory optimization for contact forces and contact-switching events while cooperating with others, enabling collaborative manipulation, robot team sports, and modular robot locomotion.

Basketball broadcast clock values are propagated between detections with the linear model T=T_0-(1/30)*n, where T_0 is the last detected time remaining and n is the number of frames elapsed at 30 fps.
Play-by-play alignment keeps candidate timestamps T'={t in T | |t-t-hat|<theta}, matching detected clock readings t against annotation timestamps t-hat within tolerance theta.

The temporal grounding pipeline extracts time-remaining and quarter values from basketball broadcast footage by fine-tuning an out-of-the-box object detector to find semantic text regions directly (no explicit game-clock localization), aligning a pre-labeled play-by-play corpus to video frames; interpolation and parallelization make it cluster-deployable and the code is public.

Soft quantization for regression-as-classification is q_i(y,tau)=exp(-||y-c_i||/tau)/sum_j exp(-||y-c_j||/tau), which converges to hard assignment q_i in {0,1} as tau->0, so hard quantization (E_q=||y-y-hat||, y-hat=argmin_{c_i}||y-c_i||) is the tau=0 special case of soft quantization.

Each prototype c_i owns a Voronoi region R_i={s: ||s-c_i||<=||s-c_j|| for all j} with volume A_i=integral_{R_i} dV; region probability factorizes as P(y in R_i)=p_i*A_i and the model outputs P-hat[y in R_i|x]=exp(f(x;theta)_i+log A_i)/sum_j exp(f(x;theta)_j+log A_j).
equation: \hat{P}[y\in R_{i}\mid x]=\frac{\exp(f(x;\theta)_{i}+\log A_{i})}{\sum_{j}\exp(f(x;\theta)_{j}+\log A_{j})},\quad P(y\in R_{i})=p_{i}\cdot A_{i}

claim: Prototype training minimizes L=L_CE+lambda_q*L_q+lambda_rep*L_rep: cross-entropy L_CE=sum_i q_i(y,tau)*log P-hat[y in R_i|x] for the density estimator, quantization loss L_q=min_{c_i}||y-c_i|| pulling prototypes to data, and repulsion L_rep=sum_{i!=j} max(0,||c_i-c_j||-delta_rep) keeping prototypes at least delta_rep apart.

Prototypes are added adaptively where usage U(c_i)=(1/|D_tr|)sum_{y in D_tr} q_i(y,tau) exceeds delta_add, sampling c_{K+1}~N(c_i,sigma^2) and concatenating C=concat(C,{c_{K+1}}); underused prototypes are deleted and others relocated during training.

The conformal prediction set is Gamma_{1-alpha}(x)=sup{R_{pi_i}: sum_{i=1}^r [y in R_{pi_i}]>=1-alpha, p(x)_{pi_i}<=p(x)_{pi_{i+1}}} ordered by ascending estimated density, with threshold q-hat_alpha=quantile(S(y_cal,x_cal)|D_cal, ceil(1-alpha+1/(|D_cal|+1))) giving the finite-sample guarantee 1-alpha<=P(Y_{n+1} in Gamma)<=1-alpha+1/(|D_cal|+1).

The conformalized high-density quantile regression method with dynamically adaptive prototypes (adding, deleting, relocating quantization bins) achieves valid coverage focused on highest-probability-density regions with fewer prototypes and less memory than fixed-bin classification-style quantile regression, scaling to higher dimensions.

IMUDiffusion's forward noising for IMU time series is x_{k,t}=sqrt(1-beta_{k,t})*x_{k,t-1}+sqrt(beta_{k,t})*eps with eps~N(0,I), t in {N | 0<t<=T}, and sinusoidal time embeddings TE_t=[sin(t/10000^{i/t_dim}),cos(t/10000^{i/t_dim})].
IMUDiffusion was trained with beta_Acc=9e-4, beta_Gyro=6e-4, learning rate eta=4e-4, smooth L1 loss with beta_{L1}=1.0, dropout p=0.3, and L2 regularization lambda=1.

Augmenting the real IMU dataset with IMUDiffusion synthetic multivariate time series improved the baseline human-activity classifier's macro F1-score by almost 30% in the best cases, showing diffusion-generated kinematic data captures realistic human activity dynamics.

Time2Vec encodes time as t2v(tau)[i]=omega_i*tau+phi_i for i=0 and F(omega_i*tau+phi_i) for 1<=i<=k, giving the Pose2Trajectory transformer a learnable periodic plus linear time representation for tennis trajectory prediction.

Tennis player trajectory error is measured by Mean Euclidean Displacement Error MEDE=(sum_{t=1}^T sqrt((x_t-x-hat_t)^2+(y_t-y-hat_t)^2))/T, the average per-frame Euclidean distance between predicted and true centroid positions.

Pose2Trajectory trains an encoder-decoder transformer on body-joint geometry plus ball positions to predict a tennis player's future trajectory (Adam beta_1=0.9, beta_2=0.98, epsilon=1e-9, MSE loss, dropout and weight decay), aimed at automated close-up camera tracking; the authors generated a dataset of bounding boxes, joints and ball positions from singles matches.

Cumulative regret is R_T=sum_{t=1}^T(mu_{a*}-E[Y|A=a_t])=T*mu_{a*}-sum_{t=1}^T E[Y|A=a_t] with a*=argmax_a mu_a; ignoring missing outcomes or assuming random missingness biases reward estimates and can cause linear regret.

Under MCAR with observation probability gamma (positivity assumption P(O^Y_t=1|M_t,A_t=a)>0), the adapted UCB achieves E[R_T]=O(sqrt(alpha*n*T*log(T)/gamma)) and no policy can beat Omega(sqrt(n*T/gamma)), so missingness inflates regret by 1/sqrt(gamma).

With a mediator M and missingness model MAR, arm means are identifiable by inverse-propensity weighting mu_a=E[sum_m 1{M_t=m}Y^o_t 1{O^Y_t=1}/gamma_{m,a}|A_t=a] with gamma_{m,a}=P(O^Y=1|m,a); the estimator is mu-hat_a=(1/|T_a|)sum_{t in T_a}(sum_m 1{M_t=m}/|T_{m,a,o}| sum_{t' in T_{m,a,o}} Y^o_{t'}).

Under MNAR with a completeness condition on P(M,Y,O^Y=1|a), the missing mass is recovered via P(m,O^Y=0|a)=integral_y P(m,y,O^Y=1|a)*P(O^Y=0|y,a)/P(O^Y=1|y,a) dy, i.e. reweighting observed outcomes by the missingness odds ratio; MAR regret lower bound is Omega(sqrt(T*n*H)) with H the harmonic mean of per-arm observation odds, and violating MAR gives linear Omega(T) regret.

A real-world MAR bandit simulation on the Mayo Clinic Primary Biliary Cirrhosis dataset (418 observations, 1974-1984) treats treatment arm Z1 as the bandit action, survival days X as the reward, and death/censoring indicator D as the mediator; the MAR algorithm's results match the synthetic-data behavior at horizon T=100000 over 10 repetitions.

The lexical ratio treats each asset as a document of sector/financial keywords and computes the normalized Shannon entropy of the portfolio-weighted term distribution: LR=-(1/log m)sum_{k=1}^m (sum_i w_i c_{i,k}/sum_i sum_j w_i c_{i,j})*log(sum_i w_i c_{i,k}/sum_i sum_j w_i c_{i,j}), where w_i are weights and c_{i,k} term counts.

The lexical ratio is scale invariant: multiplying all weights by c>0 as w'_i=c*w_i leaves every ratio unchanged because c cancels in numerator and denominator, so LR'=LR; the paper also proves concavity and maximality properties.

For comparison the paper uses the VaR diversification ratio DR_VaR(w)=VaR_alpha(w^T X)/sum_i w_i VaR_alpha(X_i) at alpha=0.05, the Azadkia-Chatterjee dependence measure T_n=sum_i(min{R_i,R_{M(i)}}-min{R_i,R_{N(i)}})/sum_i(R_i-min{R_i,R_{N(i)}}), and a risk-adjusted lexical ratio LR_risk=(-sum_j p_j log p_j)/log(m).

Empirical tests on S&P 500 portfolios show the lexical ratio aligns with conventional diversification metrics while capturing unique textual diversification dimensions, and it outperforms Markowitz volatility-based measures and diversification ratios in optimizing risk-adjusted returns, especially under varied market conditions; the relation Metric_t=beta_0+beta_1*LR_t+epsilon_t is used for evaluation.

CausalStock's evidence lower bound over the latent temporal causal graph G is log p_theta(y_T|X_{<T})=log integral_G (q_phi(G)/q_phi(G)) p_theta(y_T|X_{<T},G) p(G) dG >= E_{q_phi(G)}[sum_i log p_{z_i}(z^i_T)+log p(G)-log q_phi(G)]+H(q_phi(G)), and the training loss is L=(1/D)(-ELBO+lambda*BCE(g_T,y_T)).

The variational causal-graph posterior factorizes over lags and stock pairs as q_phi(G)~prod_l prod_i prod_j B(1,sigma_{l,ji}), a product of Bernoulli distributions where G_{l,ji}=1 means a causal link X^j_{t-l}->X^i_t at lag l; the functional causal model predicts f_i(Pa^i_G(<T))=Sigmoid(zeta_i(sum_l sum_j G-hat_{l,ji} ...)) with likelihood p_theta(y^i_T|Pa)=p_{z_i}(z^i_T)|dF_i/dz^i_T|^{-1} and |dF_i/dz^i_T|^{-1}=1.

CausalStock (lag-dependent temporal causal discovery + additive-noise functional causal model + LLM-based Denoised News Encoder) beats strong baselines on six real datasets from US, China, Japan and UK markets: with news, ACL18 accuracy 63.42+-0.0039 and MCC 0.2172+-0.0017 versus CMIN 62.69/0.2090; without news, KDD17 accuracy 56.09+-0.0069, MCC 0.1235+-0.0189; best hyperparameters lr=1e-5, L=5, lambda=0.01.

The discovered causal strengths correlate with company market values with Spearman correlations 0.7939 (ACL18, p=0.006), 0.7212 (NI225, p=0.0185), 0.6491 (CMIN-CN, p=0.0036), 0.8909 (FTSE100, p=0.0005), supporting the economic plausibility of the learned temporal causal graphs.

Global tracklet association builds a distance matrix D_{i,j}=1 if i!=j and tracklets overlap in time (Pi_i cap Pi_j != empty), else the mean pairwise appearance distance (1/(N_i N_j))sum_{i in Pi_i}sum_{j in Pi_j}(1-(F^i_m . F^j_n)/(||F^i_m|| ||F^j_n||)) using cosine distance of re-ID features.

Spatial gating for tracklet merging uses thresholds theta_hor=beta*Delta_{max,hor} and theta_ver=beta*Delta_{max,ver} with spatial factor beta in (0,1]; pairs are forbidden (D_{i,j}=1) when the bounding-box-center displacement Delta_{i,j,hor} exceeds theta_hor.

GTA (Global Tracklet Association) is a plug-and-play refinement for any multi-object tracker that splits tracklets containing multiple identities and merges tracklets of the same identity using appearance distances plus spatial constraints; it set a new state of the art on SportsMOT with HOTA 81.04% and lifted multiple trackers on SoccerNet from HOTA 79.41% to 83.11%.

SoccerGuard is an injury-prediction framework for women's professional soccer that ingests subjective wellness and training-load reports, objective GPS sensor measurements, third-party player statistics, and medically verified injury reports through preprocessing into automated machine learning plus a Soccer Dashboard GUI.

SoccerGuard experiments over synthetic data generation settings, input/output window sizes, and ML model choices show that injury event prediction can be done with considerable accuracy given the right configurations and feature combinations.

The motion diffusion model forward process is q(x_t|x_0)=N(alpha_t x_0, sigma_t^2 I) with alpha_t in (0,1) decreasing monotonically and the variance-preserving constraint alpha_t^2=1-sigma_t^2; the diffusion prior loss is L_Diff(phi,x)=E_{t,eps}[w(t)||eps_phi(alpha_t x+sigma_t eps,t)-eps||^2_2].

DiffOpt represents motion with SMPL parameters theta_{1:T} in R^{24x3xT} (joint angles), phi_{1:T} in R^{3xT} (global root orientation), x_{1:T} in R^{3xT} (root translations), and jointly optimizes the motion-prior loss with the reprojection loss L_2D=(1/T)sum_t rho(j_t,j-tilde_t) to disentangle human motion from dynamic-camera motion.

DiffOpt (Diffusion Optimization) uses a pretrained human motion diffusion model as a strong motion prior to optimize monocular global human mesh recovery, fixing artifacts like foot sliding from unmodeled root translation; validated on EMDB and Egobody, it beats state-of-the-art global HMR methods, most prominently on long videos.

The paper builds a Python linear-programming lineup optimizer for FanDuel daily fantasy baseball to test how accurate FanDuel's default lineup-optimization strategy is, aiming to propose a more accurate model to assist daily fantasy participants in selecting winning lineups.

The league-wide shift-ban effect is estimated by difference-in-differences: theta-hat=E[Y_{j,1,2023}-Y_{j,1,2022}]-E[Y_{j,0,2023}-Y_{j,0,2022}] under assumptions (1) consistency/no anticipation, (2) no spillover, (3) parallel trends E[Y_{j,1,t}-Y_{j,1,t-1}]=E[Y_{j,0,t}-Y_{j,0,t-1}] for t>=2023.

Player-level effects use synthetic control: theta-hat_{j,n,t}=Y_{j,1,n,t}-Y-hat^0_{j,1,n,t} with Y-hat^0_{j,1,n,2023}=sum_{m=1}^{58} w_{j,n,m} Y_{j,0,m,2023}, donor weights nonnegative summing to 1 (sum_m w_{j,n,m}=1), a separate weight set per target player and outcome, targeting the ATT for that player-year-outcome.

Quasi-experimental result: MLB's 2023 infield shift ban raised batting average on balls in play and on-base percentage for left-handed batters by about nine points league-wide (difference-in-differences); synthetic control analyses found several individual players gained over 70 points in OBP, OPS or wOBA from the ban, while other previously high-shift players saw little effect.

Sensitivity analyses: an in-unit check reruns the procedure on 25 players with 2022 shift rates between 15% and 30% as targets (expected noticeably smaller effects), and an in-time check pretends 2022 was the intervention year (dropping 2022 pre-intervention data and 2022-based covariates, using 2021 player age instead).
SMGDiff weights ball influence by proximity: w_b=1-||b_p^{xy}-h_p^{xy}||/r, where b_p^{xy} and h_p^{xy} are ball and human xy positions and r is a radius.

SMGDiff training losses: L_pos=(1/F)sum_i||FK(x_0^i)-FK(x-hat_0^i)||^2_2 (forward-kinematics joint positions), L_vel=(1/(F-1))sum_i||(x_0^{i+1}-x_0^i)-(x-hat_0^{i+1}-x-hat_0^i)||^2_2 (velocities), L_foot=(1/(F-1))sum_i||(FK(x-hat_0^{i+1})-FK(x-hat_0^i))*c_g^i||^2_2 (foot-ground contact), combined as L=L_simple+lambda_pos L_pos+lambda_vel L_vel+lambda_foot L_foot.

Ball-foot contact is detected as c-hat_b=I(||b_a||>tau_a) with ball-acceleration threshold tau_a=2; the contact guidance loss is L=sum_i d^i*I(d^i>tau_d)*c-hat_b^i/(I(d^i>tau_d)+delta) with contact-distance threshold tau_d=0.1m, steering denoising along D*=-sqrt(n)*sigma_t*grad_{X_t^F}L(X-hat_0^F)/||grad L||_2 blended as D=D_t+w_r(D*-D_t) with guidance rate w_r=0.5 and update X_{t-1}^F=mu_t+sqrt(n)*sigma_t*D/||D||.

SMGDiff is a two-stage real-time controllable soccer motion generator: stage 1 maps coarse user controls to diverse global character trajectories, stage 2 uses a transformer-based autoregressive diffusion model conditioned on the trajectory, plus inference-time contact guidance for realistic ball-foot interaction; it contributes a 1.08M+ frame soccer motion dataset and outperforms existing methods on motion quality and condition alignment.

LLaMo aligns text and motion with cross-attention A=Softmax(F_T W_Q (F-tilde_M W_K)^T/sqrt(d)) where F-tilde_M in R^{T x H} are enhanced motion features, F_T in R^{L x H} text embeddings, and W_Q,W_K in R^{H x d} projections.

LLaMo builds multi-scale motion features with local temporal windows W_k={j: |j-k|<=r_k*T}, segment-averaged pooled features F_M^{seg}={F-bar_M(n)}_{n=1}^N, and bidirectional fusion F_fusion=[F_T;{F_M(k)}_{k in K}] concatenating text with selected motion segments.

Instruction tuning minimizes negative log-likelihood L=-(1/N)sum_i sum_t log p(y-hat_t^{(i)}|y-hat_{1:t-1}^{(i)},F_fusion^{(i)}) over ground-truth description tokens conditioned on the fused motion-text representation.

LLaMo (Large Language and Human Motion Assistant) keeps motion in its native form rather than tokenizing it into language tokens for instruction tuning, preserving motion-specific detail; it processes video, motion and text jointly and was evaluated on high-complexity human behavior and professional activity domains including sports analytics.

Gender-specific graph neural networks predict soccer counterattack success better than architecturally identical gender-ambiguous models; trained on 20,863 frames of algorithmically identified counterattack sequences from 632 games (MLS 2022, NWSL 2022, international women's soccer 2020-2022) combining StatsPerform event data with SkillCorner spatiotemporal tracking data.

Permutation feature importance on the counterattack GNNs ranks byline-to-byline speed, angle to the goal, angle to the ball, and sideline-to-sideline speed as the node features with the highest impact on predicting counterattack success in both men's and women's soccer; data, code and the unravelsports Python package are open-sourced via the U.S. Soccer Federation GitHub.

Localized Spatial Conformal Prediction targets P(Y(s_{n+1}) in C-hat_n(X(s_{n+1})))>=1-alpha at unobserved spatial locations, with interval C-hat_n(X_{n+1})=[f-hat(X_{n+1})-Q-hat_n(1-alpha), f-hat(X_{n+1})+Q-hat_n(1-alpha)] where Q-hat_n(p)=inf{e: (1/n)sum_i 1{eps-hat(s_i)<=e}<=p} is the empirical quantile of nonconformity scores.

The tightest conformal interval shifts the quantile window: [f-hat(X(s_{n+1}))+Q-hat_n(beta*), f-hat(X(s_{n+1}))+Q-hat_n(1-alpha+beta*)] with beta*=argmin_{beta in [0,alpha]}(Q-hat_n(1-alpha+beta)-Q-hat_n(beta)).

LSCP localizes the quantile to the spatial neighborhood N(s_{n+1}): Q-hat_n(p)=inf{e: sum_{i in N(s_{n+1})} omega_i 1{Y-tilde(s_i)<=e}<=p}, learning the conditional residual distribution from neighbor residuals X-tilde(s_i)=(eps-hat(s_{j1}),...,eps-hat(s_{j|N(s_i)|})) with Y-tilde(s_i)=eps-hat(s_i); a scaled nonconformity option is eps-hat(s_i)=|(Y_i-f-hat(s_i,X(s_i)))/sigma-hat(s_i,X(s_i))|.

Spatial dependence is formalized by the mixing coefficient alpha-tilde(T1,T2)=sup{|P(A cap B)-P(A)P(B)|: A in F_Z(T1), B in F_Z(T2)} with alpha(a;b)<=alpha_1(a)g(b) and lim_{a->inf} alpha_1(a)=0; LSCP assumes stationarity and spatial mixing instead of i.i.d., and proves conditional coverage converges as |P(Y_{n+1} in C-hat_{t-1}(X_{n+1})|X_{n+1})-(1-alpha)|<=4L_{n+1}delta_n+6M_n n^{(1+gamma)/2}+(4+2M+4sqrt(M)g(b))n^{-2gamma/3}(log_2 n+2)^{4/3}.

On synthetic and real spatial data, Localized Spatial Conformal Prediction achieves accurate coverage with tighter and more consistent prediction intervals than Kriging (which relies on normality assumptions that fail at scale) and standard conformal methods.

Selective classification risk for GNN node classification with reject option is r(f,g|S_n)=((1/n)sum_i l(f(h_i),y_i)g(h_i))/phi(g|S_n), the loss averaged only over accepted nodes, with empirical coverage phi(g|S_n)=(1/n)sum_i g(h_i); the model f maps to the K-simplex Delta_{K-1} and g in {0,1} is the selection (accept/reject) function.

NCwR optimizes E(f,g)=r(f,g|S_n)+lambda*Psi(c-phi(g|S_n)) with Psi(a)=max(0,a)^2 enforcing target coverage c, blended with the full-coverage loss as E=alpha*E(f,g)+(1-alpha)*E(f); the paper uses a GAT with LeakyReLU (alpha=0.2), lambda=32, and convex combination weight alpha^l=0.5, with rejection implemented via a (K+1)-dimensional simplex output.

NCwR is the first GNN node-classification method with an integrated reject option (cost-based NCwR-Cost and coverage-based NCwR-Cov), evaluated on Cora, Citeseer and Pubmed plus the ILDC legal-judgment-prediction dataset modeled as node classification over legal cases with citation edges; abstained cases are interpreted by visualizing which input features drove the rejection. On UCI Thyroid at rejection cost d=0.05, NCwR-Cost reaches 96.56+-0.68% accuracy at 60.52+-9.21% coverage while NCwR-Cov reaches 99.66+-0.09% accuracy.

Topic-level sentiment analysis of news articles shows that sentiment scores of news on different topics (sports, politics, markets and others) each have a significant impact on the movement of the Nifty 50 market index, going beyond prior work that used only single-stock news or overall sentiment scores; presented at IEEE SILCON 2024.

Sequential positivity is diagnosed against thresholds P(A_2=1|A_1=0,L_2,W,d_2=1)>beta (static monotone), P(A_2=1|A_1,L_2,W,d_2=1)>beta (static non-monotone), and the dynamic versions P(A_2=1|A_1=0,L_2,W,d_2(L_2)=1)>beta, with the positivity hyperparameter beta=5/(sqrt(n_t) ln n_t) shrinking with the subset sample size n_t; sPoRT tuning uses alpha=0.05, beta=5/(sqrt(n_t) ln n_t), gamma=2.

Applied to longitudinal HIV treatment data, the regression-tree diagnostic (sPoRT) found no positivity violations at one or three months, but at six months flagged subgroups such as CD4c_0<1600 and CD4%_0>=30 (estimated probability 0.023, n=43, 5.4% of subset) and at nine months CD4%_4 in [25,30[ with CD4c_0 in [900,1225[ (probability 0.000, n=35, 6.2%), identifying subpopulations where treatment strategies lack support.

Regression trees provide nonparametric diagnostics of sequential positivity violations in longitudinal causal inference, handling static and dynamic treatment regimes and monotone/non-monotone treatment patterns, pinpointing subpopulations defined by covariate thresholds where causal contrasts are not identified.

A regression-based approach predicts sports TV viewership from Reddit social media engagement metrics, using user-generated content as a proxy for audience interest to optimize ad sales and revenue forecasting; the TV viewership dataset and modeling code are publicly available.

Adaptive constructive coalition manipulation lets coalition players choose each round which games to throw based on who advanced: an adaptive strategy is xi: C x [log n] x (N union {perp})^n -> {0,1} mapping coalition player, round, and current seeding to a throw/play decision, versus non-adaptive xi: C x N -> {0,1} fixed before the tournament.

The best achievable winning probability for the designated player is t_opt=argmax_{t in [0,1]}{(N,C,e*,...)}, and the dynamic program initializes M[0,{e*}]=1 and fills M[i,S]=sum over valid predecessor sets, with joint advancement probabilities p(S,S',S*,c)=prod_{e in S* cap C} c(e)*p(e,...).

Adaptive coalition manipulation in knockout tournaments is hard for every complexity class in the polynomial hierarchy (Sigma^P_k=NP^{Sigma^P_{k-1}}, Pi^P_k=coNP^{Sigma^P_{k-1}}, PH=union_k(Sigma^P_k union Pi^P_k)), yet solvable in polynomial time for constant coalition size and fixed-parameter tractable in coalition size plus the size of a minimum player set hitting every non-deterministic game; the paper also handles imbalanced tournament trees.

This is the first work to introduce adaptiveness into coalition manipulation of knockout tournaments: coalition members observe each round's advancement and then decide which games to throw to maximize a designated player's winning probability above a threshold, in the standard probabilistic setting with pairwise win matrix P_N=[p(i,j)] in Q[0,1]^{n x n} satisfying p(i,j)+p(j,i)=1 and n=2^r players.

Survey perspective on human action recognition: event cameras capture pixel-level brightness changes with high temporal precision, offering an alternative vision modality; the core difficulty versus image classification is temporal analysis over consecutive frames, compounded by computational cost and lack of adaptability of current methods.

The survey argues ethical influence should shape human action recognition: since one user's acceptable surveillance process may violate another's rights, methods should be adaptable to users' needs and requirements, and ethical boundaries should provide moral awareness to improve society's trust.

LLM pairwise consistency score: asking an LLM n times whether mu_i causes mu_j, with m 'True' responses, gives C_{i->j}=m/n; the semi-complete graph S keeps edge X_i->X_j iff C_{i->j}>=C_{j->i}, and breaking cycles uses reversal cost B_{i->j}=xi-C_{i->j}+C_{j->i}.
equation: C_{i\rightarrow j}=\frac{m}{n},\quad B_{i\rightarrow j}=\xi-C_{i\rightarrow j}+C_{j\rightarrow i}

claim: Causal-order quality is measured by D-hat_top=(1/|E|)sum_{u in V}sum_{v in Desc_G(u)} 1(v not in Desc_{G-hat}(u)), the fraction of true descendant relations missed by the estimated order; lower is better, and inconclusive runs (cycles or non-termination) are scored at maximum error and marked with tensor (x) symbols in tables.

The maximally-consistent-acyclic-tournament method (LCOS) recovers plausible causal orders from LLM consistency scores more robustly than full DAG discovery: on benchmarks it reaches e.g. best D-hat_top 1.0 on Asia, average 0.97+-0.02 on Child, 1.0+-0.0 on Covid 3 and average 0.70+-0.0 on Sachs, versus NOTEARS and GES baselines, and was also tested on real epidemiology and public health datasets.

The paper models dynamic semantic intentions in group trajectory prediction as a cooperative game using the Banzhaf interaction of a coalition [{i,j}]: I([{i,j}])=sum_{C subset of N\{i,j}} p(C)[phi(C cup [{i,j}])-...] with uniform sampling likelihood p(C)=1/2^{n-2} over subsets C of the remaining agents N\{i,j}.

Trajectory generation is diffusion-based: denoised trajectory at step tau is y-hat^{tau}=(1/sqrt(alpha_tau))(y-hat^{tau+1}-(1-alpha_tau)/sqrt(1-alpha-bar_tau)*eps-hat^tau_theta)+sqrt(1-alpha_tau)*z with alpha-bar_tau=prod_{i=1}^{tau} alpha_i, and the noise loss is L_noise=||z-f_eps(y^{tau+1},tau+1,f_theta(X,L^{-T_obs+1:0}))||_2.

Guided sampling blends noise prediction and group-condition guidance as f_eps(y,G)=f_eps(y,A)+s_g*grad_y log p(y|G) with the comprehensive condition vector G=[g_1;g_2;...;g_N] in R^{N x D_g}; training also minimizes a multi-sample uncertainty loss L_unc=(sum_s||Y-Y-hat^s||_2)/(sigma^2_theta S)+log sigma^2_theta plus tactic and Banzhaf-interaction losses L_tactic+beta*L_bi weighted by eta and alpha.

A diffusion-based multi-object trajectory prediction framework integrates group-level interactions into a conditional diffusion model, capturing cooperation trends with Banzhaf game-theoretic interaction and fusing semantic intentions with agent embeddings via global and local aggregation; the authors expand the NBA SportVU dataset with human annotations of team-level tactics and report diverse trajectory generation aligned with specific group activity.

The ensemble CRPS loss is CRPS({x_j}_{j=1}^M,y)=(1/M)sum_j|x_j-y|-(1/(2M^2))sum_j sum_k|x_j-x_k|, and the fair version removes finite-ensemble-size bias: fCRPS({x_j}_{j=1}^M,y)=(1/M)sum_j|x_j-y|-(1/(2M(M-1)))sum_j sum_k|x_j-x_k|.

To avoid the degeneracy of the fair CRPS, the paper introduces the almost-fair CRPS afCRPS_alpha:=alpha*fCRPS+(1-alpha)*CRPS=(1/M)sum_j|x_j-y|-(M-1+alpha)/(2M^2(M-1))sum_j sum_k|x_j-x_k|=(1/M)sum_j|x_j-y|-(1-eps)/(2M(M-1))sum_j sum_k|x_j-x_k| with eps:=(1-alpha)/M, a hyperparameter alpha in (0,1] where alpha=1 is the fair CRPS; training uses afCRPS with alpha=0.95, AdamW, learning rate 1e-5, batch size 16.

AIFS-CRPS is a variant of ECMWF's AI Forecasting System trained with the almost-fair-CRPS proper-score loss instead of a deterministic loss; the trained model is stochastic and generates as many exchangeable ensemble members as desired at inference; for medium-range forecasts it outperforms the physics-based IFS ensemble for the majority of variables and lead times, and for subseasonal forecasts it outperforms the IFS ensemble before calibration and is competitive when forecasts are evaluated as anomalies removing model-bias influence.

FACTS preprocesses video frames by uniform temporal subsampling X_sub={x_i | i=k*T/N}, k=0,..., and standardization X_std=(X-mu)/sigma with mean mu and std sigma for training stability before the transformer.

FACTS is a transformer-based fine-grained action classifier for close-combat sports that processes raw video directly with no pose estimation or body sensors, reaching 90% accuracy on fencing actions and 83.25% on boxing actions; it ships a new public dataset of 8 detailed fencing actions for sports analytics.

A privacy-preserving knee rehabilitation case study converts mobile phone exercise videos into diagnostic time series with Google MediaPipe pose estimation, overlaying stick-figure elements on the patient while streaming knee-angle estimates to CSV for side-by-side time series plots that flag excessive knee flexion or unstable movement against a-priori knee-angle parameters.

To quantify rehabilitation adherence, an adaptive algorithm correctly identifies 91.67%-100% of all knee exercises from side- and front-view videos; the design is transparent/interpretable and intended as open-source, non-vendor-locking infrastructure deployable within a national healthcare system (Accident Compensation Corporation New Zealand context).

The paper tests causal 'hangover effects': whether in-game team performance declines the day after playing in a city with active nightlife, using a nightlife index (built on musicians data rather than population or drinking-establishment counts, which mis-rank cities like San Antonio and New Orleans) as a proxy for unobserved off-court partying.

Season schedule accounting used: NBA seasons have at most 82x30/2=1,230 games (with 229 missing games and at most two missing per remaining season); MLB seasons have at most 162x30/2=2,430 games with shortfalls on average; MLB back-to-back away series create a structural difference versus one-off NBA games, and next-day East-coast games are impossible from West-coast cities (Nationals, Giants, Athletics, Dodgers, Diamondbacks noted).

The rotisserie fantasy basketball objective is approximated by V=Phi(mu_D/sigma_D) with mu_D=mu_T*(|O|+1)/|O|-(|C|(|O|+1))/2-mu_L and sigma_D^2=(|O|+1)/|O|*sigma_T^2+sigma_L^2, where C is the team, O the opponents, mu_T/sigma_T^2 the mean/variance of fantasy points over category matchups, and mu_L/sigma_L^2 the mean/variance of the league's maximum score.

Category fantasy-point mean and variance: mu_T=sum_{c in C}sum_{o in O} Phi(mu_{c,o}) and sigma_T^2=sum_c sum_o Phi(mu_{c,o})(1-Phi(mu_{c,o}))+(1/2)sum_a sum_b rho_{a.b} H_T(a,b); expected maximum of |O| normal draws mu_L=MEV(|O|)*sqrt(E(sigma_M^2)), sigma_L^2=E(sigma_M^2)*MVAR(|O|).

For small correlation rho, the bivariate normal CDF approximation E(AB) ~ Phi(mu_{a.m})*Phi(mu_{b.n})+((rho_1+rho_2)/2)(phi(mu_{a.m})*phi(mu_{b.n})) gives Cov(A',B')=Phi(mu_{a,m})*Phi(mu_{b,n})+((rho_1+rho_2)/2)(phi(mu_{a,m})*phi(mu_{b,n})), since week-to-week halves A_t,B_t have covariance rho_1/2 and A_m,B_n have rho_2/2, so total Cov(A,B)=(rho_1+rho_2)/2.

The tractable rotisserie approximation carries an implicit mechanism rewarding balanced teams: variance terms of the form Phi(1-Phi) are maximized at Phi=1/2, so maximizing V favors matchups the team wins with middling probability across categories; integrated into H-scoring draft simulation it performs well, with the chi=0.25 mean table reaching 64.8% average fantasy points in the 11th-year column and avoiding the poor-free-throw-shooter punts that hurt roto totals.

A gradient-of-variance identity supports optimization of the roto objective: nabla_{c,o}(sigma_T^2)=mu_{c,o}phi(mu_{c,o})[(sum_{b in C, b!=c} rho_{b,c}[-phi(mu_{b,o})-F_T(b)])+(phi(mu_{c,o})-F_T(c))]+phi(mu_{c,o})-2Phi(mu_{c,o})phi(mu_{c,o}) with F_T(c)=sum_o phi(mu_{c,o}) and nabla_{c,o}(mu_D)=((|O|+1)/|O|)phi(mu_{c,o}).

Shot quantity and quality for the home team are modeled as Gaussians with ELO-driven parameters: N(quant|mu_quant,sigma_quant^2) with mu_quant,sigma_quant=f(ELO_H,ELO_A), and likewise N(qual|mu_qual,sigma_qual^2); home goals are simulated as Home Goals=sum_{i=1}^N 1{s_i>X_i} with X_i~U(0,1) compared against simulated shot-quality draws s_i.

The method integrates established ELO ratings with machine learning models to forecast soccer match outcomes by predicting shot quantity and quality distributions rather than direct scores, and reports empirical outperformance under the Springer Soccer Prediction Challenge constraints.

Abstention rule for dynamic graph models: given input x, if abstention score a(x)<=theta then q(x)=0 (model confident) and the model predicts f(x); if a(x)>theta then q(x)=1 and the model abstains, targeting max_{f,q} P(f(x)=y | a(x)<=theta).

Coverage-based abstention objective for link prediction: L(f,q)|E_t=r-hat(f,q|E_t)+lambda*Psi(c-phi-hat(q|E_t)) with empirical selective risk r-hat(f,q|E_t)=sum_{(u,v,t) in E_t} l(f(z_u(t),z_v(t)),y_{E_t})(1-q(z_u(t),z_v(t)))/(|E_t|*phi-hat(q|E_t)), empirical coverage phi-hat(q|E_t)=(1/|E_t|)sum(1-q), Psi(b)=max(0,b)^2, and overall L_{E_t}=alpha*L(f,q)_{E_t}+(1-alpha)*L_h_{E_t}.

Node-classification abstention mirrors the edge form: L(f,q)|V_t=r-hat(f,q|V_t)+lambda*Psi(c-phi-hat(q|V_t)) with r-hat(f,q|V_t)=sum_{u in V_t} l(f(z_u(t)),y_t)(1-q(z_u(t)))/(|V_t|*phi-hat(q|V_t)) and phi-hat(q|V_t)=(1/|V_t|)sum(1-q(z_u(t))); class imbalance is handled by L_h|V_t=beta*L_h_minor|V_t+L_h_major|V_t with best results for beta in {2,5}.

This is the first reject-option framework for temporal GNNs on continuous-time dynamic graphs, covering dynamic link prediction (four datasets) and dynamic node classification (two datasets); coverage-based abstention improves AUC and average precision, e.g. DyGFormer Wikipedia AUC rising from 87.04+-1.08 at 100% coverage to 88.97+-2.37 at 80% coverage with beta=2 class weighting.

VAE evidence lower bound used in DeepDIVE: L(theta,phi;x)=E_{q_phi(z|x)}[log p_theta(x|z)]-D_KL(q_phi(z|x)||p_theta(z)), derived from log p_theta(x)=L(theta,phi;x)+D_KL(q_phi(z|x)||p_theta(z|x)) with intractable posterior p_theta(z|x)=p_theta(x|z)p_theta(z)/p_theta(x).

With latent space z=[a||b] (a reconstruction features, b forecasting features), the joint ELBO is L(theta,phi;x,y)=E_{A,B~q_phi}[log p_theta(y|a,b,x)]+E_{A,B~q_phi}[log p_theta(x|a,b)]+E_{A,B~q_phi}[log(p_theta(a,b)/q_phi(a,b|x))], and with independent priors p_theta(a,b)=p_theta(a)p_theta(b) the KL splits as D_KL(q_phi(a,b|x)||p_theta(a,b))=E_{B~q_phi}[D_KL(q_phi(a|b,x)||p_theta(a))]+D_KL(q_phi(b|x)||p_theta(b)).

The average KL to the prior decomposes as (1/n)sum_i D_KL(q_phi(z|x^{(i)})||p_theta(z))=D_KL(q_phi(z)||p_theta(z))+(log N-E_{Z~q_phi}[H(N|Z=z)]) under p_theta(z^{(i)})=p_theta(z) for all i (Hoffman & Johnson 2016 decomposition), informing the disentanglement loss derived via Naive Bayes.

DeepDIVE (Deep Disentangled Interleaving Variational Encoding) disentangles the input into marginal and conditional distributions in a VAE latent space (z=[a||b] for reconstruction vs forecasting features), fusing them by cross-attention; a theorem shows combining reconstruction and forecasting objectives fully captures the lower bound, and under a mixture-of-log-concave prior assumption the prior-posterior KL is upper bounded by a function minimized by the cross-entropy minimizer, justifying RBF plus cross-entropy with interleaving training; experiments on two public datasets beat the vanilla VAE and match state-of-the-art baselines.

Ratings initialize at mu_i=25, sigma_i=25/3 as in standard Bayesian rating systems; ratings update in a free-for-all OpenSkill setting on ML-estimated performance scores rather than game outcomes: (mu_{t+1},sigma_{t+1})=Omega_FFA(mu_t,sigma_t,PScore), with conservative single-value skill estimate theta_i=mu_i-3*sigma_i.

PandaSkill's dual rating decomposes each player's skill into context and meta components: mu_i=mu_i^{ctx}+mu_i^{meta}, sigma_i^2=(sigma_i^{ctx})^2+(sigma_i^{meta})^2, with meta updates mu_i^{meta,t+1}=(1/n)sum_j(mu_j^{meta,t+1}-theta_j^{ctx}) and sigma_i^{meta,t+1}=sqrt((1/n)sum_j(sigma_j^{meta,t+1})^2) averaging neighbors j, solving the isolated-rating-pool problem that blocks cross-regional comparison.
Win probability between players follows the Bayesian CDF rule P(S_i>S_j)=Phi((mu_i-mu_j)/sqrt(sigma_i^2+sigma_j^2)).

PandaSkill rates League of Legends players (PandaScore, IEEE submission): ML models estimate in-game performance from individual stats with each role modeled independently, then OpenSkill Bayesian updates run in free-for-all mode on performance scores instead of match outcomes, highlighting individual contributions; a dual context/meta rating system addresses fragmented competitive scenes and limited pro-game data.

Order-p Wasserstein distance between probability measures mu,nu on a Polish space: W_p(mu,nu)=(inf_{pi in Pi(mu,nu)} int_{X x X} d(x,y)^p pi(dx,dy))^{1/p}; for discrete measures it reduces to W_p^p(mu,nu)=inf_{P in R_+^{n x m}, sum_i P_{i,j}=nu_j} sum_{i,j} P_{i,j} d(x_i,y_j)^p with mu=sum_i mu_i delta_{x_i}, nu=sum_j nu_j delta_{y_j}.

For equal-size uniform discrete measures (mu_i=nu_i=1/n), Birkhoff-von Neumann reduces the Wasserstein distance to an assignment: W_p(mu,nu)=min_{sigma in S_n}((1/n)sum_i d(x_i,y_{sigma(i)})^p)^{1/p}; on the line this becomes sorted matching W_p(mu,nu)=((1/n)sum_i |x_{(i)}-y_{(i)}|^p)^{1/p}.

The sliced Wasserstein distance averages 1D Wasserstein distances over projection directions on the unit sphere: SW_p(mu,nu)=(int_{S^{d-1}} W_p^p(theta#mu,theta#nu) d theta)^{1/p}, approximated in practice by SW-hat_p(mu,nu,(theta_l)_{l<=L})=((1/L)sum_{l=1}^L W_p^p(theta_l#mu,theta_l#nu))^{1/p}, where push-forward theta#mu projects mass onto the axis theta.

For uniform discrete measures the sliced approximation collapses to a Euclidean distance between sorted-projection vectors: SW-hat_p(mu,nu,(theta_l))=((1/(nL))sum_{l=1}^L sum_{i=1}^n |<theta_l,x_{(i)}>-<theta_l,y_{(i)}>|^p)^{1/p}, giving the optimal-transport embedding mu=(1/n)sum_i delta_{x_i} |-> (<theta_l,x_{(i)}>); the paper uses deterministic grid directions theta_l=(cos(pi(l-1)/(2L)),sin(pi(l-1)/(2L))).

Playing style is characterized by a team's spatial distribution over frames: an optimal-transport embedding maps frames into Euclidean space via sliced Wasserstein distances, and quantization over frame collections yields a team similarity metric; applied to 100 games from the 2021-2022 Ligue 1 season (plus first-half 2015-2016 NBA), it retrieves relevant clusters of game situations, computes a style-similarity matrix between teams, and serves as a strong preprocessing embedding for prediction tasks.

The Plackett-Luce model for ordered hyperedges (multi-body comparisons) generalizes Bradley-Terry: P(vec-omega|vec-pi)=prod_{r=1}^{K-1} pi_{omega_r}/sum_{q=r}^{K} pi_{omega_q}, with scores pi_i=e^{s_i}>0 under the normalization prod_{i=1}^N pi_i=1, reducing to BT for K=2.

Setting the log-likelihood derivative to zero gives the fixed-point iteration pi'_s=[sum_{K,r,vec-omega in Omega^{K,r}_s} z(vec-omega)]/[sum_{K,r,vec-omega} z(vec-omega) sum_{v=1}^{r} 1/sum_{i=v}^{K} pi_{omega_i}], and Newman's accelerated variant pi'_s=[sum z(vec-omega)*sum_{i=r+1}^{K} pi_{omega_i}/sum_{i=r}^{K} pi_{omega_i}]/[sum z(vec-omega) sum_{v=1}^{r-1} 1/sum_{i=v}^{K} pi_{omega_i}]; convergence is declared when A=sqrt((1/N)sum_s(pi_s/(1+pi_s)-pi'_s/(1+pi'_s))^2)<=eps with eps=1e-6, and a logistic prior P(vec-pi)=prod_i pi_i/(1+pi_i)^2 enables MAP estimation.

The paper provides a significantly faster algorithm for Plackett-Luce ranking inference from multi-body comparisons (sports tournaments, multiplayer games, preference surveys), validated on synthetic and real data; the model is invariant under pi_i->a*pi_i scaling, which is fixed by the product-one normalization.

Goal rate is defined per match as G-bar=(1/N)sum_i G_i/T_i, and across 3,433 matches in 21 leagues the probability of a goal being scored increases as the match progresses (correlation r~0.438, p~7.13e-6), with fewer-than-expected goals in the early minutes of each half (chi^2~288.62, p=3.72e-21); this contradicts the prevailing notion of goal randomness.

The distribution of time between subsequent goals shows exponential decay, so goals cluster closer together in time; splitting by which team scores the next goal reveals bursty dynamics, with the same team more likely to score again shortly after its previous goal, implicating fatigue, tactical adaptation and psychological momentum as drivers of goal timing.

Game dynamics are x-dot(t)=f(x(t),u,v) with control inputs u in U (informed attacker) and v in V (uninformed defender); the informed player knows the payoff type i while the defender only has prior p_0 in Delta(I) updated by Bayesian rule p'(u)[i]=eta_i(u)p[i]/eta-bar(u).

Under Isaacs' condition the complexity of computing the Nash equilibrium does not depend on the action space size; the Hamiltonian is H(x,xi):=min_{u in U} max_{v in V} f(x,u,v)^T xi - l_i(u,v)=max_{v in V} min_{u in U} f(x,u,v)^T xi - l_i(u,v), and a multigrid approach reduces cost over many time steps; the DP value satisfies V_tau(t0,x0,p)=min_{{eta_i}} E_{u~eta-bar}[max_{v in V} V_tau(t0+tau,...)] with terminal boundary V_tau(T,x0,p)=sum_i p[i] g_i(x0).

Convergence theorem: there exist M1,M2>0 such that V(t0,x0,p)<=max_{zeta in Z(t0)} J(t0,x0,p,{eta_{i,tau}},zeta)<=V(t0,x0,p)+M1(T-t0)tau for any (t0,x0,p) in [0,T]xXxDelta(I), i.e. the discrete-time strategies approach the equilibrium value as tau->0; the solver scales to a 3D Hexner's game with 6D joint action, 12D state and 13D value space, with Player 1 learning to conceal his true target until a critical time.

Match win probability is pi_i=P(y_i=1|x)=h(eta_i)=h(beta_0+beta_1 x_{i1}+...+beta_p x_{ip}) with h: R->[0,1], fitted by numerical log-likelihood maximization; nonlinear effects use basis expansions f(x)=sum_j gamma_j B_j(x), and partial dependence is estimated by f-hat_S(x_S)=(1/n)sum_i f-hat(x_S,x_{i,C}).

Predictive performance uses three measures: classification rate (1/n)sum_i 1(tilde-y_i=hat-y_i) with hat-y_i=1 if hat-pi_i>0.5; predictive Bernoulli likelihood (1/n)sum_i hat-pi_i^{tilde-y_i}(1-hat-pi_i)^{1-tilde-y_i}; and Brier score (1/n)sum_i(hat-pi_i-tilde-y_i)^2, evaluated on external test data via cross-validation, rolling window and expanding window.

Statistically enhanced covariates (Elo rating plus two age variables) improve ML prediction of men's Grand Slam tennis matches: the rolling-window random forest with Points, Rank, Age.30 and Elo achieves classification rate 0.789, Bernoulli likelihood 0.659 and Brier score 0.165 (best in its table), versus Elo alone at 0.771/0.611/0.183; partial dependence and ICE plots interpret the most promising model.

Event prediction RL uses the Bellman optimality Q*(s_t,a_t)=E_{s_{t+1},r_{t+1}}[r_{t+1}+gamma max_{a'} Q(s_{t+1},a')] with TD loss L_td=sum_{t in T}(r_{t+1}+gamma*max Q - Q(s_t,a_t))^2, combined into total loss L_total=L_td+lambda_1 L_1+lambda_2 L_as; models beat baselines in action accuracy and TD loss at lambda_1=0.01 and 0.005, but only balance at 0.005 since lower values trade accuracy for TD loss (lambda_1=0.001 gives similar accuracy across MLP/GRU/LSTM).

OpenSTARLab is an open-source framework democratizing spatio-temporal soccer agent-data analysis: a Pre-processing Package standardizes event and tracking data into Unified/Integrated Event Data and State-Action-Reward formats, an Event Modeling Package implements deep-learning event prediction, and the RLearn Package supports reinforcement learning tasks.

Observed player locations are modeled as Y=Pi X where X in R^{d x 2} are role locations and Pi a hidden permutation matrix; the likelihood is a Gaussian mixture over permutations f(y,mu,Sigma,w)=sum_{Q in P_d} w_Q g(Q^T y,mu,Sigma) with g(x,mu,Sigma)=(1/((2pi)^d sqrt(prod_k det(Sigma_k))))exp(-(1/2)sum_k(mu_k-x_k)^T Sigma_k^{-1}(mu_k-x_k)).

The frame log-likelihood L_theta(y)=sum_{i=1}^n log[sum_{Q in P_d} w_Q g(Q^T y^{(i)},mu,Sigma)] is maximized after a parsimonious permutation pre-selection that discards Q when P(Pi=Q)<=o^{tresh}/2, justified by the overlap bound v(p,q)>=min(P(Pi=I_d),P(Pi=Q^T))+min(P(Pi=Q),P(Pi=I_d)) for the overlap v(p,q)=int min(p(x),q(x))dx.

A shared-component GMM gives an initial estimate: for each player l, Z_l^{(j)} has density f_l(z)=sum_{k=1}^{11} pi_{l,k} N(z|mu_k,Sigma_k) with pi_{l,k}=E(Pi_{l,k})=P(Pi_{l,k}=1); regime changes during a match are modeled by a latent regime R with X_k|R=r~N(mu_{r,k},Sigma_{r,k}) and P(Pi=Q|R=r)=w_{r,Q}, extending the log-likelihood to a double mixture over regimes and permutations.

The hidden-permutation framework disentangles player locations from role-specific positions, simultaneously estimating team formation and frame-level role assignment and capturing dynamic tactical adjustments via the latent regime variable, demonstrated on football player tracking data.

A prediction interval at confidence level 1-2alpha is Gamma_{1-2alpha}(x_t)=[q-hat_t^alpha,q-hat_t^{1-alpha}]; the quantile regression estimator is beta-hat_alpha=argmin_beta sum_t rho_alpha(y_t-x_t^T beta) with check function rho_alpha(u)=u(alpha-1{u<0}), i.e. rho_alpha(u)=alpha*u if u>=0, (alpha-1)*u if u<0.

EnbPI interval: Gamma_{1-2alpha}(x_t)=[(1/B)sum_b f^{(b)}(x_t)-lambda_t,(1/B)sum_b f^{(b)}(x_t)+lambda_t] with lambda_t=(1/B)sum_b lambda_t^{(b)}, averaging residual quantiles over bootstrap models; the final ensemble averages QR, EnbPI and SPCI: Gamma_{1-2alpha}=[(1/3)(QR^alpha+EnbPI^alpha+SPCI^alpha),(1/3)(QR^{1-alpha}+EnbPI^{1-alpha}+SPCI^{1-alpha})].

Evaluation uses the pinball score PS(q-hat_t^alpha,y_t,alpha)=(1-alpha)(q-hat_t^alpha-y_t) if y_t<=q-hat_t^alpha else alpha(y_t-q-hat_t^alpha), interval width IW_t=q-hat_t^{1-alpha}-q-hat_t^alpha, empirical coverage Lambda=(1/N)sum_t I_t^alpha with I_t^alpha=1{y_t in [q-hat_t^alpha,q-hat_t^{1-alpha}]}, and the Winkler score W_t=IW_t plus (2/tau)(q-hat_t^alpha-y_t) or (2/tau)(y_t-q-hat_t^{1-alpha}) when y_t falls outside the interval.

Conformal prediction (Ensemble Batch Prediction Intervals and Sequential Predictive Conformal Inference) gives electricity price intervals with high coverage and narrow width for day-ahead and real-time balancing markets, outperforming traditional models on validity metrics; a simulated battery-storage trading algorithm shows improved financial returns with the ensemble approach in both markets.

Inter-stock similarity combines rank correlation and sector structure: Q_{ij}^t=1-6*sum_{c=t-L+1}^{t}(R(s_i^c)-R(s_j^c))^2/(L(L^2-1)) where R(.) is the rank, and D_{ij}=1 if Se(i)=Se(j), delta_1 if Pr(i)=Pr(j), else delta_2; the adjacency is A^t=Q^t dot D, and adaptive sparsity kappa^t=tau*Sigmoid(Inception(M^t)) keeps K=|kappa^t*N^2| edges, with M^t the market index sequence.

Graph attention aggregation: alpha_{v_i,v_j}^k=exp(LeakyReLU(a_k^T[W h_i^t||W h_j^t]))/sum_{s_u^t in N(v_i)} exp(LeakyReLU(a_k^T[W h_i^t||W h_u^t])), and z_i^t=sigma(||_{k=1}^K sum_{v_j in N(v_i)} alpha_{v_i,v_j}^k h_j^t) with GELU sigma; the fused input P=Stack(s_i^t||z_i^t) in R^{N x L x 2F} feeds a multi-level Mamba with hidden state h_i^t=A-bar_i^t h_i^{t-1}+B-bar_i^t x_i^t and output o_i^t=C_i^t h_i^t.

Losses combine a pairwise-ranking regression term L_RP=(1/L)sum_t(sum_i||y_i^t-r_i^t||^2+eta*sum_{i,j}max(0,-(y_i^t-y_j^t)(r_i^t-r_j^t))) with a graph information-bottleneck term L_GIB=I(Z;X)=(1/L)sum_t sum_i ||mean(z_i^t)-mean(s_i^t)||^2/(var(z_i^t)+var(s_i^t)).

FinMamba is a market-aware Mamba-GNN for stock movement prediction that adapts inter-stock graphs to macroeconomic market conditions and mines long historical sequences efficiently; in an online deployment on the Chinese stock market (2024-01-01 to 2024-06-30, model refreshed offline weekly and trading within the first half hour of the next day's open), all model strategies significantly outperformed the market on cumulative wealth.

Conformal threshold is the (1-alpha) quantile q-hat=quantile_{ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n}{s_1,...,s_n}, giving prediction sets C(X_t)={Y' in Y: s(X_t,Y')<=q-hat} with P(Y_t in C(X_t))>=1-alpha; the paper uses two thresholds q-hat_predict=quantile({s_i},ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n) and q-hat_abstain=quantile({s_i},ceil((n+1)(1-beta))/n).

Soft action probabilities use logistic smoothing: p_single(s(x))=sigma(-c[s(x)-q-hat_predict]) and p_abstain(s(x))=sigma(c[s(x)-q-hat_abstain]) with sigma(z)=1/(1+e^{-z}); the REINFORCE policy pi_theta samples (alpha,beta)~N((mu_theta,sigma_theta^2)) and updates nabla_theta J(theta)=E_{(alpha,beta)~pi_theta}[nabla_theta log pi_theta(alpha,beta)*R(alpha,beta)] with reward R(alpha,beta)=-C(alpha,beta) and cost C(alpha,beta)=(1-acc)+lambda_1 avgSet+lambda_2 abstention, stepping theta<-theta+eta*R*nabla_theta log pi_theta(alpha,beta).

Learnable conformal abstention (CAP) treats CP thresholds as RL actions and balances accuracy, set size and abstention; across LLM/VLM benchmarks it outperforms LAC and APS, improving accuracy by up to 3.2% and boosting AUROC for hallucination detection; for LLaVA-1.6-34B, set-prediction rates range 55.4% (AI2D) to 62.4% (ScienceQA), single predictions 31.5-38.8%, and abstention 6.1% (ScienceQA) to 12.8% (AI2D).

Dual-threshold conformalization: the conformal threshold is q-hat_conf=Quantile({s_i},(n+1)(1-alpha)/n) and the abstention threshold is ROC-optimized as q-hat_abs=argmax_tau{TPR(tau)-FPR(tau)}; the prediction set is C-hat(X)={y: -log p(y)<=q-hat_conf} with coverage P(y_true in C-hat(X))>=1-alpha.

Calibration quality uses expected calibration error ECE=sum_b (|B_b|/N)*|acc(B_b)-conf(B_b)| and normalized entropy H_norm(p)=-(1/log K)sum_k p(y_k)log p(y_k), margin M(X)=p(y_(1))-p(y_(2)), set size S(X)=|{y:-log p(y)<=q-hat_conf}|, and AUC=int_0^1 TPR(tau) dFPR(tau).

Evaluated on CIFAR-100, ImageNet1K and ModelNet40 under camera/LiDAR perturbations, the dual-threshold framework achieves abstention-detection AUC 0.993->0.995 under severe conditions, maintains coverage above 90.0%, and scales adaptive abstention from 13.5% to 63.4%+-0.5 as environmental severity rises; modality-specific patterns show larger set sizes for ImageNet1K (8.81+-0.3->21.09+-0.5) than CIFAR-100 (1.90+-0.1->6.80+-0.3), with ModelNet40 most concentrated (1.20+-0.1->2.30+-0.2).

Explainable tree-based models (random forest and XGBoost) outperform alternatives on one-year-ahead forecasts of professional football player quality and transfer value from historical data-driven indicators; random forest is judged most suitable because it gives accurate predictions plus uncertainty quantification naturally arising from its bagging procedure, and the analysis shows player performance development contains nonlinearities.

The value-prediction kNN uses interpretable features including age in years, months with zero minutes played, current and lagged estimated transfer values (etv, etv_diff_6m_ago, etv_diff_12m_ago), SciSkill ratings at current/6m/12m lags, player sciskill potential and its 6-month difference, plus club 36-month fee averages and player transfer-history counts.

Match goals follow a Poisson model: team i scores k goals with probability P_{ij}(k)=(lambda_{ij}(f))^k exp(-lambda_{ij}(f))/k!, where the win expectation comes from Elo, W_{ij}=1/(1+10^{-(E_i-E_j)/400}), and the neutral-field expected goals lambda_{ij}(n) is a fitted polynomial in W_{ij} (e.g. leading term 3.90388*W_{ij}^4-0.58486*W_{ij}^3-2.98315*W_{ij}^2+...).

Stakeless matches (at least one team indifferent because already qualified or eliminated) are classified by expected cost: more costly when the indifferent team is more likely to win honestly; a novel imbalanced-groups format for the 48-team 2026 FIFA World Cup drastically reduces the probability of stakeless matches played by the strongest teams under Monte Carlo simulation, increases outcome uncertainty, and needs fewer matches (same 12x6=72 group matches but only 24 knockout games instead of 32).

MeT-Pose is a metamorphic-testing framework for pose estimation systems (sports analytics, livestock care) that bypasses the oracle problem and costly manual keypoint labeling by checking consistency of predictions across transformed inputs, letting users assess systems under application-relevant conditions (human vs animal, whole-body vs extremities) without reusable labeled test data.

Elo is the online update theta_{t+1}[i_t]<-theta_t[i_t]+eta_t(o_t-p_t), theta_{t+1}[j_t]<-theta_t[j_t]-eta_t(o_t-p_t) with p_t=sigma(theta_t[i_t]-theta_t[j_t]) and logistic loss l_t:=-(o_t ln p_t+(1-o_t)ln(1-p_t)); reinterpreted as online gradient descent on f_t with nabla_theta f_t(theta)=-(o_t-p_t)(e_{i_t}-e_{j_t}), it inherits the no-regret bound Regret_T=sum_{t=1}^T f_t(x_t)-min_{x in K} sum_t f_t(x)<=(3/2)GD sqrt(T) for step sizes eta_t=D/(G sqrt(t)), implying (1/T)Regret_T<=C sqrt(N/T).

Model misspecification is tested with the likelihood-ratio statistic Lambda:=2[min_theta L_test(theta)-min_{theta,alpha} L-tilde_test([theta;alpha])] where L-tilde uses augmented features g_t=[theta_train features] and tests H_0: alpha=0; the finding is that most practical matching datasets (including LLM arena) deviate significantly from Bradley-Terry and stationarity, yet Elo still frequently outperforms mElo and pairwise models on win-rate prediction.

Synthetic experiments on transitive but non-BT models (strong/weak stochastic transitivity: pi(i)>pi(j) implies P_{ik}>=P_{jk} for all k, resp. P_{ij}>=1/2) show the sparsity of practical matching data is the critical factor behind Elo's superiority over more complex systems; a further empirical observation is a strong correlation between Elo's predictive accuracy and its ranking performance.

Ranking inconsistency under non-uniform matchmaking: with the given P,Q the offline MLE converges to theta^mle=[5.48,0.89,4.60,0.04,0] inducing the inconsistent ranking 1 succ 3 succ 2 succ 4 succ 5, and bootstrap confidence intervals ([4.86,5.33],[0.72,1.17],[4.18,4.68],[-0.07,0.31],[0.00,0.00]) confirm the ranking 1 succ 3 succ 2 succ 4.

On-field validity of the Prevent Biometrics instrumented mouthguard in NCAA American football (35 male players, 64 player matches, video review) shows sensitivity 0.89 and positive predictive value ranging 0.76-0.98 depending on false-positive definition, supporting suitability for measuring head acceleration events in elite American football.

Head acceleration event incidence per player match: above 10 g, 11.2 (defense) and 11.3 (offense); above 30 g, 1.6 and 2.6; above 1.0 krad/s^2, 5.5 and 6.9; above 2.0 krad/s^2, 0.9 and 1.4; peak linear and angular acceleration incidences appear similar between offense and defense, providing a benchmark for position-specific interventions to reduce exposure.

BST's transformer block is X-tilde^{(l)}=X^{(l-1)}+MHSA(split(LN(X^{(l-1)}))) with per-head projections Q=[Q_1 ... Q_H]=X W_Q in R^{S x (D_A x H)} (and K,V analogously) and head_h=softmax(Q_h (K_h)^T/sqrt(D_A)) V_h; stroke-clip boundaries in rally R_i are detected by expanding frame ranges with margins epsilon and t to form C-hat^{(i)}_j.

Player-target weighting uses alpha=(alpha-tilde+2)/4 mapping alpha-tilde in [-2,2] to alpha in [0,1]; the comparison table shows e.g. TemPose-PF with joints+ball reaching 0.738/0.677/0.905 at 1.62M parameters versus SkateFormer 0.712/0.627/0.859 at 2.38M and BlockGCN 0.715/0.627/0.886 at 1.50M.

The Badminton Stroke-type Transformer classifies stroke types in singles from skeleton joints, shuttlecock trajectories and player positions (segmented by a novel racket-swing video segmentation plus pose estimation and TrackNet-style trajectory detection), and outperforms the previous state of the art on ShuttleSet, the largest publicly available human-annotated badminton video dataset; the authors argue leveraging ball trajectory is likely a trend for racket-sport action recognition.

SportsSUSHI is a hierarchical graph-based approach for long-term player tracking in team sports that leverages domain-specific features (jersey numbers, team IDs, field coordinates) to re-identify players and reconnect tracklets after extended absences or prolonged occlusions; it achieves high performance on SoccerNet and a new stationary-camera hockey tracking dataset with long sequences annotated with team IDs and jersey numbers, and dataset plus code are public on GitHub.
Move-sequence models are evaluated with fixed-length perplexity PPL(x_0,...,x_t)=exp(-(1/t)sum_i^t log(p_theta(x_i|x_{<i}))).

Three transformer models predict bouldering move sequences from simple hold-sequence information alongside an interactive visualization pipeline for move-sequence evaluation; results are not conclusive but represent a first step toward ML-based boulder move prediction (EPFL student work).

Shot locations and outcomes are modeled as a marked spatio-temporal point process with log intensity log{lambda_j(s,z_i)}=alpha_0(s)+z_i^T beta_j(s), where s is court location, z_i game covariates, and j in {0,1} marks missed/made shots; the point-process likelihood is pi(S|lambda_0,lambda_1)=prod_{i,j}{exp{|R|-int_R lambda_j(s,z_i)ds} prod_{s in s_{i,j}} lambda_j(s,z_i)}.

Spatial effects get Gaussian process priors alpha_0(s)~GP(0,sigma_0^2 kappa) and beta_{j,k}(s)~GP(0,sigma_{j,k}^2 kappa); the kernel admits eigen-decomposition kappa(s,s')=sum_l xi_l phi_l(s)phi_l(s') with orthonormal eigenfunctions, so alpha_0(s)=sum_l theta_l^0 phi_l(s), theta_l^0~N(0,sigma_0^2 xi_l), and similarly for beta_{j,k}(s).

Computation truncates to L eigenfunctions with alpha_0(s)~=phi^T(s)theta^0 and beta_{j,k}(s)~=phi^T(s)theta^beta_{j,k}, choosing L so that sum_{l=1}^L xi_l/sum_{l=1}^infty xi_l>alpha for a given alpha in (0,1); the log intensity becomes log[lambda_j(s,z_i)]=X_{i,j}^T(s)theta with theta=(theta^0,theta^{0,beta T},theta^{1,beta T})^T~N(0,Sigma), Sigma=diag{sigma_0^2,sigma_beta^2 I_{2p}} tensor Xi, Xi=diag{xi_1,...,xi_L}; the kernel used is kappa(s,s')=exp{-a(||s||^2+||s'||^2)-b||s-s'||^2} with sigma_{jk}^2=sigma_beta^2 for all j,k.

A Bayesian log Gaussian Cox process with spatially varying coefficients jointly models shot-attempt locations and make/miss outcomes across games, estimating spatial relative risk under different covariate values via a kernel-convolution MCMC; a case study on Stephen Curry, LeBron James and Michael Jordan shows how playing conditions, game location and opposing-team strength shift shooting efficiency across court regions.

Using pre-season smartwatch sensor data and ecological momentary assessments, a machine-learning model distinguishes 14 collegiate volleyball players who go on to perform well versus poorly with leave-one-subject-out cross-validated F1 score 0.75, enabling targeted interventions before the season starts.

Correlations with hit performance: perceived performance (rho=0.346, p=0.002), breathing rate most significant feature (F=60.780, p<0.001), reception errors negatively correlated (rho=-0.288, p=0.012), perceived stress negatively correlated, perceived soreness positively correlated (rho=0.169, p=0.045); skill improved significantly over the season (beta=0.0040, p=0.003) with setters showing a significant negative interaction term (beta=-0.0040, p=0.013).
GoalNet propagates on event-centric graphs via H^{(l+1)}=sigma(A H^{(l)} W^{(l)}), pools the graph as z=(1/|V|)sum_v h_v, and predicts expected-threat change as y-hat=W_4 dot ReLU(W_3 dot z).

Individual credit for xT change is assigned by xT_v=||h_v^{(L)}||/sum_u ||h_u^{(L)}|| * Delta xT with Delta xT=xT_current-xT_previous; attention variants use alpha_uv=exp(LeakyReLU(a^T[W h_u||W h_v]))/sum_{w in N(v)} exp(...) (GAT) and alpha_uv=exp((q_u.k_v+r_uv)/sqrt(d))/sum_w exp((q_u.k_w+r_uw)/sqrt(d)) (graph transformer).

GoalNet is a GNN framework that assigns individual credit for changes in expected threat (xT) to highlight pivotal non-scoring players (ball-retaining defenders, defensive midfielders) that attacking-centric metrics overlook; it encodes spatial and temporal features in event graphs with centrality-aware embeddings, tests GAT and transformer variants for long-range dependencies, and is validated on real match data.

Movement counts follow the Dirichlet-multinomial f_DM(y_i|alpha)=int f_M(y_i|N_i,pi) f_D(pi|alpha) dpi=Gamma(N_i+1)Gamma(sum_j alpha_j)/(Gamma(N_i+sum_j alpha_j) prod_j Gamma(y_ij+alpha_j)/(Gamma(alpha_j)Gamma(y_ij+1))), with concentration parameters in log-linear form alpha_j=eta(x_i):=exp(beta_{j0}+sum_{k=1}^p beta_{jk} x_{ik}), p=13 covariates; effects are flagged when |beta_{jk}/SE|>3.

Half-to-half movement distribution shifts are tested per athlete-match with the Hellinger distance between quantile-cube count distributions under the null P^{(1)}_{a,m}=P^{(2)}_{a,m}, using Bonferroni-corrected significance alpha-hat=0.05/g; the quantile cube segments elite female soccer athletes' GPS movement (23 matches, n=396 vectorized cubes) into velocity, acceleration and movement-angle quantiles, revealing significant individual half-to-half differences, PCA-identified anomalous games at season start/end, and position/playing-time/game-characteristic effects on movement profiles.

The vote-share deviation from true probability follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck SDE d(Z(n,q)-q)=-(1/(n+1)) r_inf(n)(Z(n,q)-q) dn+(b(q)/(n+1)) dW(n,q) with diffusion b(q)=sqrt(q(1-q))/Delta t; r_inf(n) is the fraction of informed bettors in interval n.

The mean squared error converges as MSE(Z(n,q),q)=E[(Z(n,q)-q)^2]=MSE(Z(1,q),q)exp(-2 int_1^n r_inf(m)/(m+1) dm)+int_1^n exp(-2 int_l^n r_inf(m)/(m+1) dm) q(1-q)/((l+1)^2 Delta t) dl, showing crossover from power-law to accelerated exponential convergence; empirically r_inf(n)=0.334+(n-1)/49*0.658 with R^2=0.90 on 3,450 Japan Racing Association 2008 races.

JRA odds follow O=max(1.1,0.788/Z) with vote share recovered as Z(r,h,n)=C/(O(r,h,n)+0.05), normalized time n[r,i]=100*t[r,i]/T[r] in [0,100]; the framework treats herders (bets following current odds) and informed bettors (wagering on true win probability) analogously to noise and fundamentalist traders in financial markets.

TrackID3x3 introduces TI-HOTA, a tracking-identification metric: TI-HOTA=(1/19)sum_{alpha in {0.05,...,0.95}} sqrt(DetA_alpha x AssA_alpha) with DetA_alpha=|TP|/(|TP|+|FP|+|FN|) and AssA_alpha=(1/|TP|)sum_{c in TP} A(c); pose-aware HOTA uses HOTA(P,G)=LocSim(P,G) x IdSim(P,G) with LocSim(P,G)=e^{ln(0.05)*||P-G||_2^2/tau^2}.

TrackID3x3 is the first public comprehensive dataset for multi-player tracking, identification and pose estimation in 3x3 basketball (indoor fixed-camera, outdoor fixed-camera, drone subsets); baselines at tau=0.5 show indoor TI-HOTA 80.75+-13.16 (DetA 79.46, AssA 82.11) versus outdoor 46.11+-20.55, and outdoor HOTA for ByteTrack 47.92+-5.98 vs BoT-SORT-ReID 50.64+-3.03.

Kinematic quantities are formalized from 3D point tracks: movement direction angle theta_t=arccos(((P_{t+1}^{(i)}-P_t^{(i)}) dot (P_{s+1}^{(i)}-P_s^{(i)}))/(||P_{t+1}^{(i)}-P_t^{(i)}|| ||P_{s+1}^{(i)}-P_s^{(i)}||)) and traveled distance sum_{t=s}^{e-1}||P_{t+1}^{(i)}-P_t^{(i)}||_2.

ST-VLM (kinematic instruction tuning) gives vision-language models spatio-temporal reasoning via STKit and STKit-Bench: real-world videos with 3D annotations detailing traveled distance, speed, movement direction, inter-object distance comparisons and relative movement direction, plus an automatic pipeline generating pseudo-labels for videos without 3D labels using real-world-scale 4D reconstruction; ST-VLM achieves outstanding performance on STKit-Bench (applications: autonomous driving, sports analytics).

A method collects simulated soccer tracking data from the Google Research Football environment to develop continuous tracking-data models, storing it in a schema representative of real tracking data with processes extracting high-level features and events; examples of established tracking-data models demonstrate efficacy, addressing the scarcity of publicly available tracking data (AAMAS 2025 demo track).

CSPO (Cross-market Synergy with Pseudo-volatility Optimization) forecasts stock price movements by enriching stock embeddings with forward-looking external futures-market knowledge to capture stock exogeneity, and by modeling stock-specific forecasting confidence with pseudo-volatility to address volatility heterogeneity, enabling dynamically adaptive optimization; extensive industrial and public benchmark experiments show superiority over existing methods (ACM Web Conference 2025 companion).

Distributional regression with reject option lets a model abstain from estimation under high uncertainty at a fixed rejection rate; the optimal rule has a closed form that thresholds the entropy function of the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS), and a semi-supervised procedure estimates both the conditional distribution function and the CRPS entropy function on labeled data while calibrating the desired rejection rate on unlabeled data.

Rejection-rate control in this framework is distribution-free; under mild conditions the procedure is asymptotically as effective as the optimal rule in error rate and rejection rate, with rates of convergence established for distributional k-nearest neighbor, and strong performance is shown in numerical analysis on real-world datasets.

The expected-goals wordalisation pipeline builds an xG model by logistic regression: log-odds(x)=beta_0+sum_j beta_j x_j and P(y=1|x)=1/(1+e^{-log-odds(x)}); each feature's contribution is Contribution of x_j=beta_j*x-tilde_j with x-tilde_j=x_j-mu_j, and additive attributions follow g(z')=phi_0+sum_i phi_i z'_i.

Wordalisations use LLMs to turn xG model coefficients (distance, angle, defensive pressure) into entertaining natural-language shot descriptions for coaching and commentary, documented in a model card with an open-source Streamlit app (shotsgpt.streamlit.app) that imports user shot datasets and explores xG explanations interactively; the approach generalizes to other football actions.

A review of proper scoring rules covers their mathematical foundations including general characterization results and important families of scoring rules, their dual role in statistics and machine learning as evaluation tools for probabilistic forecasts and as methods for estimating probability distributions, and interesting recent developments in their usage across applications.

A survey of Action Valuation in sports analytics introduces a taxonomy with nine dimensions covering data, methodological approaches, evaluation techniques and practical applications of assigning scores to individual actions by their contribution to desired outcomes, identifying essential characteristics of effective methods, research gaps and future directions.

A dynamical model of player and ball motion mathematically encodes hypotheses about player behavior and interactions in a three-versus-one ball possession game; model plausibility is checked by comparing simulated outcomes with experimental results, and sensitivity analysis estimates causal effects of interventions, finding causal effects of behavioral aspects such as pass speed and accuracy on team effectiveness.

Draft pick value follows the two-parameter Massey-Thaler exponential (Weibull-type) curve v_n(alpha,beta)=e^{-lambda(n-1)^{beta}}; trade fairness equates aggregated pick values as Value(team X's draft picks)=v_{j_1}+v_{j_2}+...+v_{j_m}~approx v_{k_1}+...+v_{k_n}=Value(team Y's draft picks), with the p-norm aggregation Value(team X)=(sum_{i=1}^m (e^{-lambda(j_i-1)^{beta}})^p)^{1/p}~approx (sum_{i=1}^n (e^{-lambda(k_i-1)^{beta}})^p)^{1/p}.

The trade discrepancy to minimize is Delta=(sum_i (e^{-lambda(j_i-1)^{beta}})^p)^{1/p}-(sum_i (e^{-lambda(k_i-1)^{beta}})^p)^{1/p}; L1 norm ||x||_1=sum_i|x_i| (convex, nondifferentiable at zero, sparsity-promoting) and L2 norm ||x||_2=sqrt(sum_i x_i^2) (convex and differentiable off-origin, gradient-friendly) represent aggressive top-heavy versus balanced risk-averse draft philosophies, fitted by L-BFGS-B from initial [0.146,0.698] on 2006-2023 NFL trade data with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals for lambda,beta; code at github.com/tanmay-sketch/draftdynamics.

SpineTrack is the first comprehensive 2D spine pose dataset in unconstrained settings, annotating nine detailed spinal keypoints (vs the single rigid segment used by prior datasets) across a synthetic set of 25k annotations from Unreal Engine with OpenSim biomechanical alignment and a real-world set of over 33k annotations from an active-learning pipeline; SpinePose extends SOTA body pose estimators with knowledge distillation and anatomical regularization to jointly predict body and spine keypoints, validated in general and sports contexts.

A 3D human pose estimation framework for combat sports with sparse multi-camera setups integrates transformer-based top-down multi-view 2D tracking with epipolar constraints and long-term video object segmentation for identity consistency, weighted triangulation plus spline smoothing for initial 3D poses, kinematic optimization, and a multi-person physics-based trajectory optimization step handling rapid motion, occlusions and close interactions; it achieves state-of-the-art results including on a new elite boxing benchmark, with annotated video datasets released.

F3Set is a benchmark for fast, frequent, fine-grained (F3) event detection in video (e.g. sports actions suffering motion blur and subtle visual differences), containing datasets with usually over 1,000 event types, precise timestamps and multi-level granularity; popular temporal action understanding methods were evaluated revealing substantial challenges, and the new F3ED method achieves superior performance; dataset, model and benchmark code are public on GitHub.

GridMind is a multi-agent NLP framework unifying structured, semi-structured and unstructured NFL data (statistics, sensor data, articles, audio, video) through Retrieval-Augmented Generation and large language models to enable natural-language cross-modal data insights in real-time sports analysis (Telemetry Sports).

A benchmark evaluation methodology combines Item Response Theory with the Glicko-2 rating system (rating, deviation, volatility updated via simulated tournaments between classifiers) to jointly account for dataset complexity and algorithm generalization; an OpenML-CC18 case study shows only 15% of datasets are truly challenging, a reduced 50% subset offers comparable evaluation power, and Random Forest achieved the highest ability score.
